• and His saying in al-Baqarah: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: You shall not worship except Allah, and to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83], the verse;

• وقَوْلِهِ في سُورَةِ لُقْمانَ: ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِي ولِوالِدَيْكَ إلَيَّ المَصِيرُ﴾ [لقمان: ١٤]، وبَيَّنَ في مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ أنَّ بِرَّهُما لازِمٌ ولَوْ كانا مُشْرِكَيْنِ داعِيَيْنِ إلى شِرْكِهِما؛

• and His saying in Surat Luqman: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final destination﴾ [Luqman: 14]. And He explained in another place that their dutifulness is binding even if they are polytheists calling to their polytheism;

• كَقَوْلِهِ في ”لُقْمانَ“: ﴿وَإنْ جاهَداكَ عَلى أنْ تُشْرِكَ بِي ما لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ فَلا تُطِعْهُما وصاحِبْهُما في الدُّنْيا مَعْرُوفًا﴾ [لقمان: ١٥]،

• such as His saying in "Luqman": ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ [Luqman: 15];

• وقَوْلِهِ في ”العَنْكَبُوتِ“: ﴿وَوَصَّيْنا الإنْسانَ بِوالِدَيْهِ حُسْنًا وإنْ جاهَداكَ لِتُشْرِكَ بِي ما لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ فَلا تُطِعْهُما إلَيَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ﴾ الآيَةَ [العنكبوت: ٨] .

• and His saying in "al-'Ankabut": ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents; but if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. To Me is your return﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 8], the verse.

وَذِكْرُهُ جَلَّ وعَلا في هَذِهِ الآياتِ بِرِّ الوالِدَيْنِ مَقْرُونًا بِتَوْحِيدِهِ جَلَّ وعَلا في عِبادَتِهِ، يَدُلُّ عَلى شِدَّةِ تَأكُّدِ وُجُوبِ بِرِّ الوالِدَيْنِ. وجاءَتْ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ في ذَلِكَ أحادِيثَ كَثِيرَةٍ.

His mention, majestic and exalted, in these verses of dutifulness to parents coupled with His oneness in worship indicates the great emphasis on the obligation of dutifulness to parents. And many hadiths have come from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this matter.

وَقَوْلُهُ جَلَّ وعَلا في الآياتِ المَذْكُورَةِ: ﴿وَبِالوالِدَيْنِ إحْسانًا﴾ [الإسراء: ٢٣] بَيَّنَهُ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿إلّا إيّاهُ وبِالوالِدَيْنِ إحْسانًا إمّا يَبْلُغَنَّ عِنْدَكَ الكِبَرَ أحَدُهُما أوْ كِلاهُما فَلا تَقُلْ لَهُما أُفٍّ ولا تَنْهَرْهُما وقُلْ لَهُما قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا﴾ ﴿واخْفِضْ لَهُما جَناحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ وقُلْ رَبِّي ارْحَمْهُما كَما رَبَّيانِي صَغِيرًا﴾ [الإسراء: ٢٣ - ٢٤]؛ لِأنَّ هَذا مِنَ الإحْسانِ إلَيْهِما المَذْكُورِ في الآياتِ، وسَيَأْتِي إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ تَعالى إيضاحُ مَعْنى خَفْضِ الجَناحِ، وإضافَتِهِ إلى الذُّلِّ في سُورَةِ ”الشُّعَراءِ“، وقَدْ أوْضَحْنا ذَلِكَ غايَةَ الإيضاحِ في رِسالَتِنا المُسَمّاةِ ”مَنعَ جَوازِ المَجازِ في المَنزِلِ لِلتَّعَبُّدِ والإعْجازِ“ .

His saying, majestic and exalted, in the aforementioned verses: ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-Isra': 23] is clarified by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except Him, and to parents, good treatment. If one of them or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff" and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy on them as they brought me up when I was small"﴾ [al-Isra': 23-24]; because this is part of the good treatment toward them mentioned in the verses. And it will come, God willing, the explanation of the meaning of "lowering the wing" and its being attributed to humility, in Surat "ash-Shu'ara'". We have explained that thoroughly in our treatise entitled "Man' Jawaz al-Majaz fi al-Manzil lil-Ta'abbud wal-I'jaz" (The Prohibition of the Permissibility of Metaphor in the Revelation for Worship and Inimitability).

(p-٨٦)وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ الكَرِيمَةِ: ﴿وَقَضى رَبُّكَ﴾ [الإسراء: ٢٣] مَعْناهُ: أمَرَ وألْزَمَ، وأوْجَبَ ووَصّى ألّا تَعْبُدُوا إلّا إيّاهُ.

(p-86) His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isra': 23] means: He commanded, obligated, required, and enjoined that you not worship except Him.

وَقالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: ﴿وَقَضى رَبُّكَ﴾ [الإسراء: ٢٣]، أيْ أمَرَ أمْرًا مَقْطُوعًا بِهِ، واخْتارَ أبُو حَيّانَ في ”البَحْرِ المُحِيطِ“ أنَّ إعْرابَ قَوْلِهِ: إحْسانًا أنَّهُ مَصْدَرٌ نائِبٌ عَنْ فِعْلِهِ، فَهو بِمَعْنى الأمْرِ، وعَطْفُ الأمْرِ المَعْنَوِيِّ أوِ الصَّرِيحِ عَلى النَّهْيِ مَعْرُوفٌ؛ كَقَوْلِهِ:

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isra': 23], i.e., He commanded a definitive command. Abu Hayyan, in "al-Bahr al-Muhit" (The Surrounding Sea), chose that the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying "ihsanan" (good treatment) is that it is a verbal noun (masdar) substituting for its verb, so it carries the meaning of a command. The coordination of an implied or explicit command with a prohibition is well known, as in his saying:

؎وُقُوفًا بِها صَحْبِي عَلى مَطِيِّهِمْ يَقُولُونَ لا تَهْلَكْ أسًى وتَجَمَّلِ

Stopping there, my companions upon their mounts, saying: "Do not perish from grief, but bear up with dignity."

وَقالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ في الكَشّافِ: ﴿وَبِالوالِدَيْنِ إحْسانًا﴾ أيْ: وأحْسِنُوا بِالوالِدَيْنِ إحْسانًا، أوْ بِأنْ تُحْسِنُوا بِالوالِدَيْنِ إحْسانًا.

Al-Zamakhshari said in "al-Kashshaf": ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-Isra': 23], i.e., "and be good to your parents with good treatment," or "by your being good to your parents with good treatment."

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾

The pronoun in His words ﴿from them﴾ [al-Isra: 28] refers to those mentioned before it in His words: ﴿And give the relative his right, and the poor, and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Isra: 26]. The meaning of the verse is: If you turn away from these mentioned persons and do not give them anything, because you do not have it, and your turning away from them is ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾ [al-Isra: 28], that is, lawful provision, like spoils (fay') which Allah provides for you, and then you give them from it, then ﴿speak to them a gentle word﴾, that is, soft, kind and good, such as praying for them to be made wealthy and to have abundant provision, and promising them that when Allah grants you provision from His bounty, you will give them from it.

This is a great instruction from Allah to His Prophet in noble character: if he is not able to give graciously, then let him adorn his refusal, for a graceful refusal is better than an ugly giving.

What this noble verse indicates has been stated explicitly by Allah, the Exalted, in Surah al-Baqarah in His words: ﴿A kind word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 263]. Indeed, one who said it excelled:

Though if there is no silver that I can one day give to the askers, then I am gentle in my manner (lit. "pliant of stick").

The askers will never lack good from my character, whether it is my giving or the goodness of my refusal.

The noble verse points out that he ﷺ would not turn away from giving except when there was nothing to give from, and that when Allah makes the awaited provision easy, he gives them from it and does not turn away from them. This is the utmost of generosity and nobility of character. Al-Qurtubi said: "qawlan maysuran" is a verbal noun used in the sense of an active participle, from the root "yusr" (ease), like "maymun" (blessed).

From what we have established, it is known that His words ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Isra: 28] are connected to the conditional verb, which is ﴿turn away﴾ (tu'ridanna), not to the conditional response (jaza').

Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, permitted its connection to the response and its placement before it. The meaning of that: "then speak to them a gentle word seeking mercy from your Lord," that is, be easy with them and kind to them, seeking by that the mercy of Allah. Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr al-Muhit, rejected this, saying that what follows the response particle (fa’) does not govern what comes before it. He said: "It is not permissible in your saying, 'in yaqum fadrib Khalidan' (if he stands, then strike Khalid), to say: 'in yaqum Khalidan fadrib' (if he stands Khalid, then strike). This is explicitly stated," end of quote.

On the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah have mercy on him: the pronoun in His words ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ [al-Isra: 28] refers to the disbelievers; that is, if you turn away from the disbelievers seeking mercy from your Lord, that is, victory for you over them, or guidance from Allah for them. According to this, the "gentle word" is tact in speech, as stated by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, end of quote from al-Bahr. "Yasara" with light (non-doubled) form is both intransitive and transitive, and "maysur" is from the transitive; you say: "yassartu laka kadha" when I prepared it for you; Abu Hayyan also stated this.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 33 (part 1 of 7):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing; indeed, he is supported.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, exalted and majestic, makes clear that whoever is killed wrongfully, Allah has given his heir authority (sultan), forbids him from excess in killing, and promises him that he is supported.

The prohibition of excess in killing here covers three forms:

The first: that he kills two or more persons in return for one, as the Arabs used to do in the Jahiliyyah. An example is the saying of Muhalhil ibn Rabi'ah when he killed Bujayr ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abbad in the well-known War of al-Basus: "Pay back with the thong of Kulayb's sandal." Al-Harith ibn 'Abbad became angry and recited his famous ode:

"Bring close to me the tethering place of the ostrich; the war of Wa'il has given birth, after gestation."
"Bring close to me the tethering place of the ostrich, for the exchange of nobles for a sandal's thong is costly," etc.

Muhalhil also said:

"Every slain man of Kulayb was deceived, until the family of Murrah obtains a killing."

It is known that killing a group for one person who did not share in killing him is excess in killing, included in the prohibition mentioned in the verse.

The second: that he kills only one person in return for the slain, but a person other than the killer, because killing an innocent for the sin of another is excess in killing, which is also forbidden in the verse.

The third: that he kills the killer himself and mutilates him, for the addition of mutilation is also excess in killing.

This is the verified meaning of the noble verse. As for what some scholars have mentioned, and what al-Razi inclined to somewhat in his tafsir, that the meaning of the verse is: the wrongdoing killer should not commit excess in killing, out of fear of the authority and the support that Allah has granted to the heir of the slain, its weakness is not hidden, and it does not fit with His saying after it: ﴿indeed, he is supported﴾ [al-Isra': 33].

This authority that Allah has granted to the heir of the slain is not explained here in detail, but He indicated in two places that this authority is the power granted by Allah to the heir of the slain over the killer, by enabling him to kill him if he wishes; this does not preclude that if he wishes he may pardon for blood-money or without compensation.

The first: His saying here: ﴿let him not commit excess in killing﴾ [al-Isra': 33] after mention of the aforementioned authority, because the prohibition of excess in killing, linked to the mention of the aforementioned authority, indicates that the aforementioned authority is that very killing in which excess is forbidden.

The second place: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And for you in retribution is life, O people of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178–179]. It indicates that the aforementioned authority is what is contained in this verse of retaliation, and the best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

* *

Issues related to this noble verse

The first issue: From His saying "wrongfully" it is understood that whoever is killed other than wrongfully, his heir has no authority over his killer. This is so, because whoever is killed by right, his blood is lawful, and his heir has no authority to kill him, as we have previously cited the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, agreed upon, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The blood of a Muslim man who testifies that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah is not lawful except in one of three cases: the married adulterer, a life for a life, and one who abandons his religion and separates from the community." As previously explained in Surah al-Ma'idah.

And we explained this understanding in His saying "wrongfully," which also makes clear the understanding in His saying (p-89) ﴿and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Isra': 33].

Know that some evidences have reported other causes for permitting the killing of a Muslim beyond the three mentioned, with scholars differing on this. Among them: the highwaymen (muharibun) who have not killed anyone, according to those who say that the Imam has the choice among the four matters mentioned in His saying: ﴿that they be killed or crucified﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Ma'idah: 33], as previously explained in full in Surah al-Ma'idah.

Among them: the killing of the one who commits and the one with whom it is committed in the sin of sodomy (liwat), and we have previously presented the opinions on this and their evidences with clarification in Surah Hud.

As for killing the sorcerer, it is not far-fetched that he is included in killing the apostate mentioned in His saying: "one who abandons his religion and separates from the community," due to the Qur'an's indication of the disbelief of the sorcerer in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But Solomon did not disbelieve; rather, the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 102],
• and His saying: ﴿And they do not teach anyone until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 102],
• and His saying: ﴿And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them. And they had already known that whoever purchases it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102].

As for killing one who withholds zakat: if he denies its obligation, he is a disbelieving apostate, included in "one who abandons his religion and separates from the community." But if he withholds it while acknowledging its obligation, what is permitted regarding him is fighting, not killing, and between fighting and killing there is a clear and well-known difference.

As for what some scholars have mentioned, that whoever has intercourse with an animal is to be killed, and the animal is killed with him, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has intercourse with an animal, kill him and kill the animal with him." Al-Haythami said in Majma' al-Zawa'id: It was narrated by Abu Ya'la, and in its chain is Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn 'Alqamah, whose hadith is good, and the rest of its narrators are trustworthy; and Ibn Majah narrated it through Dawud ibn al-Husayn from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Most scholars hold that he is not killed, because restricting what makes the blood of a Muslim lawful to the three mentioned in the agreed-upon hadith of Ibn Mas'ud takes precedence over this hadith, along with the great severity in the Book and the Sunnah regarding killing a Muslim without right, and other matters mentioned in the branches of law.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: This restriction to the three mentioned in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud (p-90), which is established in the Sahih, should not be added to, except for what is established by revelation with a certainty free from objection, given its strength. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

The second issue: Other verses have come indicating that one killed by mistake does not fall under this ruling;
• such as His saying: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have done by mistake, but for what your hearts have intended﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5],
• and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make mistakes﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 286], because of what is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayrah: "that when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it, Allah said: 'Yes, I have done so.'"
• and His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾ [al-Nisa': 92], then He explained what is required of the one who kills by mistake:
• by His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake - then the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation (diyah) delivered to his family, unless they give it as charity﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 92].

The Prophet (ﷺ) has explained the diyah in amount and kind, as is known in the books of hadith and jurisprudence, as will be explained later.

* *

The third issue: From the unrestricted wording of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully﴾ [al-Isra': 33] it is understood that the ruling of the verse applies equally to killing by a sharp instrument, such as a weapon, and by a non-sharp object, such as crushing the head with a stone and the like, because all of this is truly called killing wrongfully, so retaliation (qisas) is obligatory.

This is the view of the majority of scholars, including Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad in the more correct of his two reports.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh Muslim: It is the position of the majority of scholars.

Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, disagreed on this issue and said: Retaliation is obligatory only for killing by a sharp instrument specifically, whether it is of iron, stone, or wood, or in what is known as a means of killing people, such as the catapult (manjaniq) and throwing into fire.

The majority argued that one who intentionally kills by a non-sharp instrument is subject to retaliation, with evidences:

The first: what we have mentioned of the unrestricted wording of the texts on this.

The second: the well-known hadith of Anas ibn Malik, which al-Shaykhan and the rest of the group narrated: "that a Jew killed a girl for her ornaments, crushing her head with stones. He confessed to that, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) killed him between two stones, crushing his head between them."

This agreed-upon hadith is a clear, sound text on the point of dispute, and it establishes the proof against Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, especially against his position on the equality of the blood of a Muslim and a disbeliever who is protected, such as a dhimmi.

(p-91) The third: what Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and others narrated from Hamal ibn Malik concerning retaliation for killing with a miswak-like stick (al-mistah). Al-Nasa'i said: Yusuf ibn Sa'id informed us, saying: Hajjaj ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Amr ibn Dinar informed me that he heard Tawus narrate from Ibn 'Abbas, from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "that he asked about the judgment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in that matter, and Hamal ibn Malik stood and said: 'I was between two women, one of them struck the other with a mistah and killed her and her unborn child,' so the Prophet (ﷺ) judged regarding her unborn child a ghurrah, and that she be killed for it." Abu Dawud said: Muhammad ibn Mas'ud al-Mis-sisi narrated to us, Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj who said: 'Amr ibn Dinar informed me that he heard Tawus, from Ibn 'Abbas, from 'Umar: that he asked about the judgment of the Prophet (ﷺ) in that matter, and Hamal ibn Malik ibn al-Nabighah stood and said: "I was between two women, one of them struck the other with a mistah and killed her and her unborn child, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) judged regarding her unborn child a ghurrah, and that she be killed." Abu Dawud said: al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-Mistah is the sawlaj (a stick with a curved head). Abu Dawud said: Abu 'Ubayd said: al-Mistah is a piece of the tent's poles. Ibn Majah said: Ahmad ibn Sa'id al-Darimi narrated to us, Abu 'Asim narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj informed me, 'Amr ibn Dinar narrated to me that he heard Tawus, from Ibn 'Abbas, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, that he asked the people about the judgment of the Prophet (ﷺ) in that matter (meaning regarding the unborn child), and Hamal ibn Malik ibn al-Nabighah stood and said: "I was between two of my wives, one of them struck the other with a mistah and killed her and killed her unborn child, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) judged regarding the unborn child a ghurrah of a slave, and that she be killed for it." End of quotation from the three Sunan, with their wording.

It is not hidden that this chain is sound. The narration of Abu Dawud from Muhammad ibn Mas'ud al-Mis-sisi, who is Ibn Mas'ud ibn Yusuf al-Naysaburi, also called al-Mis-sisi, Abu Ja'far al-'Ajami, resident of Tarsus and al-Misisah, is a trustworthy and knowledgeable narrator. The narration of Ibn Majah from Ahmad ibn Sa'id al-Darimi, who is Ibn Sa'id ibn Sakhr al-Darimi, Abu Ja'far, is a trustworthy and retentive narrator. Both of them (I mean Muhammad ibn Mas'ud mentioned by Abu Dawud, and Ahmad ibn Sa'id mentioned by Ibn Majah) narrated this hadith from Abu 'Asim, who is al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad ibn al-Dahhak ibn Muslim al-Shaybani, Abu 'Asim al-Nabil, a trustworthy and firm narrator. Al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn Jurayj, who is 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Jurayj, a trustworthy, jurist, and virtuous narrator, who used to commit tadlis and irsal; however, in this hadith he explicitly stated hearing and informing from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who is trustworthy and firm, from Tawus, who is trustworthy, a jurist, and virtuous, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Hamal, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p-92) As for the narration of al-Nasa'i, it is from Yusuf ibn Sa'id, who is Ibn Sa'id ibn Muslim al-Misisi, a trustworthy and retentive (thiqah hafiz) transmitter, from Hajjaj ibn Muhammad, who is Ibn Muhammad al-Misisi al-A'war, Abu Muhammad al-Tirmidhi by origin, who settled in Baghdad and then in al-Massisa. He is trustworthy and firm (thiqah thabt), but he became confused (ikhtalata) toward the end of his life when he came to Baghdad before his death. He narrates from Ibn Jurayj, and the rest of the sanad (chain of narrators) is as mentioned in the works of Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah. This hadith was not confused by Hajjaj in his narration of it from Ibn Jurayj, as shown by the narration of Abu 'Asim from Ibn Jurayj, which he transmitted in Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah in the same way as Hajjaj's narration in al-Nasa'i. Abu 'Asim is trustworthy and firm.

It was narrated by al-Bayhaqi from Abd al-Razzaq, from Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Hajar, in al-Isabah, in the biography of Hamal (the narrator mentioned), definitively affirmed the soundness of this chain. Al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra regarding this hadith: "This is a sound chain." Also, al-Tirmidhi, in his book al-'Ilal, reported that he said: "I asked Muhammad (i.e., al-Bukhari) about this hadith, and he said: 'This is a sound hadith. It was narrated by Ibn Jurayj from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jurayj is a memorizer (hafiz).'" End of quotation.

This hadith is therefore a strong text on retaliation (qisas) for killing with an instrument other than a sharp one, since the mistsah is a pole. Al-Jawhari said in his al-Sihah: "The mistsah is also the pole of a tent." The poet, who is Malik ibn Awf al-Nasri, said:

"Dayṭar of Khuza'ah confronted us, but what good is a dayṭar who turns a mistsah over?"

He means: these people confronted us to fight us, but they were nothing, for they had no weapon except the mistsah and the dayṭar. The dayṭar is a large man who has no strength (ghina) to offer.

The fourth point: the apparent meanings of verses of the Book of Allah indicate retaliation for killing with a blunt instrument. Such as the saying of Allah, Exalted:

• ﴿Whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194], the verse.
• And His saying: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [al-Nahl: 126].
• And His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].
• And His saying: ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with and then is oppressed, Allah will surely aid him﴾ [al-Hajj: 60], the verse.
• And His saying: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those have no ground of blame against them. The blame is only against those who wrong people﴾ [al-Shura: 41-42], the verse.

In al-Muwatta' there is the following text: "Yahya narrated to me from Malik, from Umar ibn Husayn, the client of Aisha bint Qudamah, that Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan gave the guardian of a man retaliation against a man who had killed him with a staff. So the guardian killed him with a staff." (p-93)

Malik said: "The matter agreed upon, about which there is no disagreement among us, is that if a man strikes a man with a staff, or throws a stone at him, or strikes him intentionally and he dies from that, this is intentional killing, and retaliation is required for it." Malik said: "Intentional killing, according to us, is that a man intends to a man and strikes him until his soul departs." End of the relevant point of the quotation.

We have already mentioned that this view, that retaliation applies to killing with a blunt instrument, is the view held by the majority of scholars, including the Four Imams, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, Ibn Sirin, Hammad, Amr ibn Dinar, Ibn Abi Layla, Ishaq, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. Ibn Qudamah transmitted this from them in al-Mughni.

Abu Hanifa, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ata and Tawus, may Allah have mercy on them, disagreed with this. They said: there is no retaliation for killing with a blunt instrument. They argued for this with evidences:

Among them: retaliation requires intent (al-'amd), and intent is one of the actions of the heart. It is known only through decisive indicators that point to it. If the killing was with an instrument of killing, such as a sharp one, it is known that he intended to kill. If it was by other means, his intent to kill is not known, because it is possible that he intended only to wound him or to hurt him without intending to kill him, so it reverts to quasi-deliberate killing (shibh al-'amd).

Among them is what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided concerning the fetus of a woman from the Banu Lihyan, which was stillborn, that a ghurrah (a slave or slave-girl) be given. Then the woman against whom the ghurrah was decreed died, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided that her inheritance belongs to her children and her husband, and that the blood money ('aql) is upon her 'asabah (paternal kin)."

In another narration: "Two women of Hudhayl fought, and one of them struck the other with a stone and killed her and what was in her womb. They brought the dispute to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he decided that the blood money for her fetus is a ghurrah, a male or female slave, and he decided the blood money for the woman upon her 'aqilah (paternal kin)."

They said: "This is a hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh), which indicates the absence of retaliation for killing with a non-sharp instrument, because the narrations of this hadith indicate killing with a non-sharp instrument: in some of them, she killed her with a mi'mud (pole), and in some, she killed her with a stone."

Among them is what was reported from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, Abu Hurayrah, Ali and Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with them, as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet): that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no qawd (retaliation) except with iron (a blade)." In some of its narrations: "Everything is a mistake except the sword, and for every mistake there is an arsh (compensation)."

Some of those who supported this view from the Hanafis tried to refute the arguments of their opponents. He claimed that the Prophet's (ﷺ) crushing of the head of the Jew between two stones occurred merely on the basis of the claim of the slave-girl whom he had killed, and that this indicates that he was known for spreading corruption on earth, and for that reason the Prophet (ﷺ) did to him what he did.

And the refutation of the narration of Ibn Jurayj from Tawus from Ibn Abbas, mentioned earlier, is that it contradicts the established narrations in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim and others: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) decided the blood money upon the 'aqilah of the woman, not retaliation."

Al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra, after mentioning the soundness of the chain of the hadith from Ibn Abbas about retaliation against the woman who killed the other with a mistsah, as previously cited, the following: "However, in the wording of the hadith there is an addition that I have not seen in any of the transmission routes of this hadith, namely the killing of a woman by a woman. In the hadith of Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, connected (mawsul), and the hadith of Ibn Tawus from his father, unconnected (mursal), and the hadith of Jabir and Abu Hurayrah, connected and established, that he decided her blood money upon the 'aqilah." End of the relevant point of al-Bayhaqi's words, in his wording.

Al-Bayhaqi also mentioned that Amr ibn Dinar was challenged regarding this hadith, on the basis that Ibn Tawus narrated it from his father in a manner contrary to Amr's narration. So he said to the one who challenged him: "You have made me doubt."

The majority responded to these arguments as follows: his crushing of the head of the Jew was retaliation (qisas). In a narration established in the Two Sahihs and others, the Prophet (ﷺ) did not kill him until he confessed that he had killed the slave-girl. So it was retaliation by the confession of the killer, and this is an agreed-upon text, explicit on the point in dispute, especially according to those who hold that the blood of a Muslim and a non-Muslim protected by a covenant (dhimmi) is equal, like Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him.

They also answered the claim that intent is an action of the heart, and that one cannot know that he was intentional unless he struck with the instrument customarily used for killing, by saying: a blunt instrument such as a pole or a large rock is among the instruments of killing, like the sword, because a person whose head is crushed with a pole or a large rock customarily dies immediately, just as one struck with a sword dies. This suffices as an indicator of intent to kill.

They also answered what is established of the Prophet's (ﷺ) decision upon the 'aqilah of the woman who killed with a pole or a stone, that it is blood money, in three ways:

The first: it is contradicted by the authentic narration we have previously cited in Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Hamal ibn Malik, who was the companion of the story. In it, the killer and the killed were his two wives, and the Prophet (ﷺ) decided concerning them retaliation, not blood money.

The second: what al-Nawawi mentioned in his commentary on Muslim and elsewhere. He said: "This is to be understood as applying to a small stone and a small pole, which is not generally intended to kill, so it is quasi-deliberate killing, for which blood money is owed by the 'aqilah, and for which there is no retaliation or blood money owed by the perpetrator. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and the majority." End of al-Nawawi's words, may Allah have mercy on him.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: This answer does not seem convincing to me, because in some established narrations in the Sahih it is stated that she was killed with a pole of a tent, and restricting it to a small one that does not generally kill is far-fetched.

The third: what Ibn Hajar mentioned in Fath al-Bari, that such a woman generally does not intend to kill the other. He said the following:

"Those who held this view, meaning retaliation for killing with a blunt instrument, answered that the pole of a tent varies in size, so that some of it generally kills and some of it does not generally kill, and the principle of equivalence in retaliation is only prescribed when the offence was committed with something that generally kills."

In this answer there is room for consideration, for what appears is that retaliation was not required in it because she did not intend the like of it, and the condition for retaliation is intent, and this is only quasi-deliberate killing. Therefore there is no proof in it for killing with a blunt instrument nor for its converse. End of Ibn Hajar's words, in his wording.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: The decisive evidence that the killing of this woman of her co-wife was a mistake in killing, quasi-deliberate, because she intended to strike and not to kill, with what does not generally kill, is the explicit statement of the agreed-upon narrations that the Prophet (ﷺ) made the blood money upon the 'aqilah, and the 'aqilah does not bear intentional killing by the consensus of the Muslims.

They answered the hadith "There is no qawd except with iron" by saying that it is not established.

Al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra, after citing its routes from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, Abu Bakrah, Abu Hurayrah and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them, the following:

"This hadith has no established chain. Ali ibn Hilal al-Tahhan is abandoned (matruk), Sulayman ibn Arqam is weak, Mubarak ibn Fadalah is not to be used as a proof, and Jabir ibn Yazid al-Ju'fi is criticized." End of quotation.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, under the chapter "If he is killed with a stone or a stick," the following:

(p-96) "The Kufans disagreed and argued with the hadith 'There is no qawd except with the sword,' which is a weak hadith transmitted by al-Bazzar and Ibn Adi from the hadith of Abu Bakrah. Al-Bazzar mentioned disagreement regarding it along with the weakness of its chain. Ibn Adi said: 'All its routes are weak.' And even if it were established, it would be contrary to their principle that the Sunnah does not abrogate the Book nor specify it."

They also argued with the prohibition of mutilation (muthlah), which is authentic, but the majority understand it as referring to other than mutilation in retaliation, reconciling the two evidences. End of the relevant point of Ibn Hajar's words, in his wording.

The great scholar al-Shawkani, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said in Nayl al-Awtar the following:

"The Itrah (the Prophet's family), the Kufans, including Abu Hanifa and his companions, held that retaliation is only by the sword, and they relied on the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir in Ibn Majah, al-Bazzar, al-Tahawi, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi, with various wordings, among them 'There is no qawd except with the sword.' Ibn Majah also narrated it, as did al-Bazzar and al-Bayhaqi, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah. Al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. Al-Daraqutni narrated it from the hadith of Ali, and al-Bayhaqi and al-Tabarani from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it from al-Hasan as a mursal report.

All these routes contain, each one of them, a weak or abandoned narrator, to the extent that Abu Hatim said: 'It is a munkar hadith.' Abd al-Haqq and Ibn al-Jawzi said: 'All its routes are weak.' Al-Bayhaqi said: 'No chain has been established for it.'" End of the relevant point of al-Shawkani's words, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him.

There is no doubt about the weakness of this hadith according to the scholars of hadith. Shaykh Ibn al-Turkumani attempted to strengthen it in his marginal notes on the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi, by claiming that Jabir ibn Yazid al-Ju'fi and Mubarak ibn Fadalah were strengthened, although Jabir is weak and a Rafidi (extremist Shi'i), and Mubarak practices tadlis of the type called tadlis al-taswiyah (concealing a weak intermediary).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 33 (part 3 of 7):

Its annotator, may God pardon him, said: The view that the evidence shows to be preferable to me is that retaliation (qisas) is required absolutely for intentional killing, whether by a blunt or a sharp instrument, because of the evidences we have mentioned, and because of the saying of the Mighty and Exalted: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179], to the end of the verse. For a killer who uses a club or a large rock, if he knows that retaliation will not be taken from him, will be emboldened to kill, and so the wisdom mentioned in the saying of the Most High, ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾, to the end of the verse, is lost. And knowledge is with God, the Most High.

* *

The fourth issue: The majority of scholars hold that the authority which God gave in this verse to the guardian of the one killed unjustly entails a choice between three things: retaliation (qisas), accepting blood money (diyah) by compulsion upon the offender (al-Jani) (p-97), and pardoning without any compensation. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: "This was also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Sirin, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr." Ibn Hajar, in al-Fath, attributed it to the majority.

Malik, Abu Hanifah, and al-Thawri, may God have mercy on them, disagreed. They said: The guardian has only retaliation or a free pardon. If he pardons in exchange for blood money, and the offender says, "I will not accept anything but killing or a free pardon, and I will not accept blood money," then the guardian of the one killed has no right to force him to pay the blood money.

Know that those who said the guardian has a choice between retaliation and blood money differed about what exactly killing intentionally makes obligatory, into two opinions. The first: it is only retaliation (qawd), and on this view blood money is a substitute for it. The second: it is one of two things, either retaliation or blood money.

The fruit of this disagreement appears in the case where he pardons the offender with an unrestricted pardon, without stating that he intends blood money or a pardon of it. On the view that what is obligatory in specific is retaliation, the blood money falls away by the unrestricted pardon. On the view that what is obligatory is one of the two matters, the blood money is required despite the unrestricted pardon. But if he pardons in exchange for blood money, it is binding, and even if the offender does not consent, according to the proponents of this view. The aforementioned disagreement is two narrations from al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, may God have mercy on them both.

Those who argued that the choice between retaliation and blood money belongs to the guardian of the one killed cited the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever has a slain relative, he has the better of two options: either he takes the ransom, or he kills." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim (al-Shaykhan), Ahmad, and the authors of the Sunan, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him. However, the wording in al-Tirmidhi is: "Either he kills, or he pardons." The meaning of "yufda" in some narrations, and "yuwadda" in others, is: he takes the ransom, in the sense of blood money. His saying "yaqtul," in the active form, means: he kills the killer of his relative.

They said: This hadith, agreed upon by the scholars, is a clear text on the point in dispute, explicitly stating that the guardian of the one killed has the choice between retaliation and taking blood money, and that he may compel the offender to whichever of the two he chooses. This evidence is strong in its indication and its text, as you can see.

They also cited the saying of the Most High: ﴿But if anything is remitted to him by his brother, then pursuit should be made according to what is reasonable, and payment should be made to him in a good manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. They said: God, the Mighty and Exalted, linked the pursuit of blood money by the particle "fa" (then) to the pardon in His saying: ﴿But if anything is remitted to him by his brother, then pursuit should be made according to what is reasonable﴾, to the end of the verse. This is clear evidence that blood money becomes binding merely by the pardon, and it is also a strong Qur'anic evidence.

(p-98) Some scholars who opposed this view, such as Malik and Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on them both, argued with evidences, among them what al-Tahawi said. The proof for them is the hadith of Anas concerning the case of al-Rubayyi', his paternal aunt, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Book of God is retaliation." He ruled by retaliation and did not give a choice. Had the choice belonged to the guardian, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have informed them, since it is not permissible for a judge to rule for one who has one of two rights in favour of one of them before informing him that the right is his in either of them. When he ruled by retaliation, it became necessary to interpret his saying "he has the better of two options" to mean: the guardian of the one killed has a choice, on condition that the offender consents to be made to pay blood money. End of quotation.

Ibn Hajar, in Fath al-Bari, responded to al-Tahawi's argument with the following text: It is answered that his saying (ﷺ), "The Book of God is retaliation," was said when the guardians of the one injured in an intentional offence requested retaliation. Know that the Book of God was revealed so that when the injured party seeks retaliation, it is granted to him. There is nothing in what he claimed about delaying the explanation.

The second: what al-Tahawi also mentioned, that they agreed that if the guardian said to the killer, "I am content that you give me such and such on condition that I do not kill you," the killer is not compelled to do so, and it is not taken from him by force, even though it is obligatory for him to preserve his own life.

The third: his saying (ﷺ) in the aforementioned hadith, "He has the better of two options...," is a case of the usual course (ghalib), so it has no implied opposite meaning (mafhum mukhalafah). It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that when a text follows the usual course, it has no implied opposite meaning, because the intention may be the predominance itself, not the intention of excluding the implied meaning from the ruling of the explicit statement. For this reason, the majority of scholars did not treat the implied opposite meaning in God's saying: ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 23], since it follows the usual course. We have mentioned this matter in this blessed book several times.

The clarification of this in the hadith is that the implied opposite meaning of his saying, "He has the better of two options," is that if the offender refuses to accept blood money and puts himself forward to be killed, refusing to give the blood money, he is compelled to give it. This is because it is one of the two options between which the Lawgiver gave the guardian of the one killed a choice. The usual case is that a person prefers his own life to his wealth, and so ransoms himself from killing with his wealth. The hadith following this usual matter prevents considering its implied opposite meaning, as the scholars of jurisprudence mentioned. Al-Shanqiti (the author) put this in Maraqi al-Su'ud in his words about the impediments to considering the indication of the statement, i.e., the implied opposite meaning:

"Or ignorance of the ruling, or the speech arose in answer to a question, or it followed what is most common."

The point of evidence is his saying: "or it followed what is most common," and so on, among the other proofs they cited.

Its annotator, may God pardon him, said: The view that appears to me to be preferable by evidence on this issue is that the guardian of the one killed is the one who has the choice between the two matters. So if he wants blood money and the offender refuses, he may compel him to pay it, based on the indication of the agreed-upon hadith, and on the indication of the verse mentioned earlier, and because God says: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 29], and He says: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195].

It is clear that if he intends to destroy himself to protect his wealth for the heir, the Lawgiver prevents him from this conduct, which deviates from the path of correctness, and compels him to protect his life with his wealth.

As for what al-Tahawi cited as consensus, that if the guardian says to him, "Give me such and such in exchange for not killing you," he is not compelled to do so, it is answered that if he says, "Give me the blood money prescribed for intentional killing," he is compelled to do so, based on the explicit text of the hadith and the verse mentioned.

But if he says to him, "Give me such and such, other than blood money," he is not compelled, because that is a demand for something other than what the Lawgiver made obligatory. And knowledge is with God, the Most High.

* *

The fifth issue: The majority of scholars hold that killing has three states:

The first: intentional killing (al-'amd), which is the one in which the authority mentioned in the verse applies, as we have already stated.

The second: quasi-intentional killing (shibh al-'amd). The third: killing by error (al-khata').

Among those who held this view are the three Imams: Abu Hanifah, Ahmad, and al-Shafi'i. Ibn Qudamah, in al-Mughni, transmitted it from 'Umar and 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, and from al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, Hammad, the people of Iraq, al-Thawri, and others.

Malik, may God have mercy on him, disagreed with the majority and said: Killing has only two states. The first: intentional killing, and the second: killing by error. What others call quasi-intentional killing, he classed as intentional killing. He, may God have mercy on him, argued that God did not place in His Mighty Book any intermediary between intentional and erroneous killing, but rather the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that there is no intermediary between them, as in His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by error. And whoever kills a believer by error, then the freeing of a believing slave and blood money paid to his family﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 92]. Then He said concerning intentional killing: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and God will be angry with him and curse him﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 93]. So He did not place any intermediary between error and intention. Likewise His saying: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you did in error, but what your hearts intended﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Ahzab: 5]. He did not place an intermediary there between error and intention, even though that verse concerns something other than killing.

The majority argued that there is an intermediary between pure error and pure intention, called quasi-intentional error (khata' shibh 'amd), on two grounds:

The first: this is exactly what happens in reality. Whoever strikes with a small stick or a small stone, from which death does not usually result, intends the striking itself, believing that such a blow will not kill the one struck. So his act is quasi-intentional in terms of his intention to strike, but it is an error with respect to the killing, because he did not intend to kill; the killing occurred without his intending it.

The second: a hadith indicating this, which Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan: Sulayman ibn Harb and Musaddad, the meaning being the same, both said: Hammad narrated to us, from Khalid, from al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, from 'Uqbah ibn Aws, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said. Musaddad's version: "He addressed them on the day of the Conquest in Makkah, and said 'Allahu Akbar' three times, then said: 'There is no god but God alone, who fulfilled His promise, supported His servant, and defeated the confederates alone' (up to here I memorized it from Musaddad, then both agreed): 'Behold, every honour from the Jahiliyyah that is claimed, whether of blood or wealth, is under my feet, except the watering of the pilgrims and the keeping of the House.' Then he said: 'Behold, the blood money for quasi-intentional error is what is done with a whip and a stick: one hundred camels, of which forty are pregnant with their young.'" Musaddad's version is more complete.

Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Wuhayb narrated to us, from Khalid, with this chain, approximately the same meaning.

Musaddad narrated to us, 'Abd al-Warith narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Zayd, from al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with the same meaning, saying: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) addressed them on the day of the Conquest, or the Conquest of Makkah, from the step of the House, or the Ka'bah."

Abu Dawud said: Thus Ibn 'Uyaynah also narrated it from 'Ali ibn Zayd, from al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p-101) Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani narrated it from al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr. A narration similar to the hadith of Khalid was narrated by Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ali ibn Yazid, from Ya'qub al-Sadusi, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ). End of Abu Dawud's text, the point of purpose from his Sunan.

Al-Nasa'i narrated something similar, and mentioned the disagreement about Ayyub in the hadith of al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, and mentioned the disagreement about Khalid al-Hadhdha' in it, and went at length into that. We have omitted the wording of his statement because of its length.

Ibn Majah, may God have mercy on him, said in his Sunan: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi and Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, both said: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Ayyub: I heard al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The slain in quasi-intentional error is the slain by whip and stick: one hundred camels, of which forty are pregnant with their young."

Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, Sulayman ibn Harb narrated to us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, from 'Uqbah ibn Aws, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), similarly.

The compiler of these notes (muqayyiduhu), may Allah pardon him, said:

Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Zuhri narrated to us: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from Ibn Jud'an, who heard it from al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, from Ibn 'Umar: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the day of the Conquest of Makkah while he was on the steps of the Ka'bah. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: 'Praise be to Allah, who fulfilled His promise, granted victory to His servant, and defeated the confederates alone. Indeed, the slain by error is slain by the whip and the staff, and for him is one hundred camels, of which forty are pregnant she-camels with their young in their wombs.'" (End of quotation.)

Al-Bayhaqi (may Allah have mercy on him) gathered the chains of transmission of this hadith. After mentioning the report from Ibn 'Umar in whose chain is Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, he said: Abu 'Abdullah al-Hafiz informed us, saying: I heard Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Sukkari say: I heard Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah say: "One day I attended the assembly of al-Muzani, and a questioner from the Iraqis asked him about shibh al-'amd (quasi-deliberate killing). The questioner said: 'Allah, blessed and exalted, described killing in His Book with two descriptions: deliberate and by error. So why do you say that it is of three types? And why do you say shibh al-'amd?'"

Al-Muzani argued with this hadith. His opponent said to him: "Will you rely on Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an?" Al-Muzani fell silent. I said to his opponent: "This report has been narrated by someone other than Ali ibn Zayd." He said: "And who narrated it other than Ali?" I said: "It was narrated by Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani and Khalid al-Hadhdha'." He said to me: "Then who is 'Uqbah ibn Aws?" I said: "'Uqbah ibn Aws is a man from the people of Basra, and Muhammad ibn Sirin, with his high standing, narrated from him." He then said to al-Muzani: "Are you debating, or is this man?" Al-Muzani said: "When the hadith comes, it is the one that debates, because it knows the hadith better than I do. Then I speak." (End of quotation.) Then al-Bayhaqi began to cite the chains of the said hadith.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, said: It is not hidden from anyone with even a little knowledge of isnads (chains of transmission) that the hadith is established from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, and that the narration from Ibn 'Umar is an error, and its defect comes from Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, because he is weak.

It is well known in the sciences of hadith (mustalah al-hadith) that when a hadith comes sound through one route, it is not weakened by its also coming through another route that is not sound. The episode which al-Bayhaqi mentioned, of the debate of Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah with the Iraqi who debated al-Muzani, indicates the soundness of using the said hadith as proof according to Ibn Khuzaymah.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, said: Once you have understood the disagreement among scholars regarding the cases of killing, whether they are three or two, and once you have known the arguments of both sides, know that what the evidence indicates as stronger is the view adopted by the majority (al-jumhur), that the cases are three: pure deliberate killing ('amd mahd), pure killing by error (khata' mahd), and quasi-deliberate killing (shibh al-'amd), because of the indication of the hadith we have mentioned, and because the majority of the scholars of the Muslims adopted it. The hadith only establishes something on which the Qur'an was silent, so the most that can be said in this matter is that a matter on which the Qur'an was silent has been added by the Sunnah. This presents no problem for those who follow the principles of the Imams, except Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him), because it is established in his principles that adding to the text of the Qur'an is abrogation (naskh), and that the mutawatir (widely transmitted) is not abrogated by ahad (solitary reports), as was previously clarified in Surah al-An'am. However, Imam Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) agreed with the majority on this question, contrary to Malik, as was previously mentioned.

Given what we have established, that the cases of killing are three, know that pure deliberate killing carries retaliation (qisas). We have already mentioned the ruling on pardon in it. Killing by error is quasi-deliberate killing. Pure killing by error, in both of these, carries blood money (diyah) payable by the 'aqilah (the paternal kin who bear the obligation).

* *

The scholars differed regarding the age categories of the blood money in these two cases. We shall explain, if Allah the Exalted wills, the amounts of blood money in pure deliberate killing when the victim's heirs pardon in return for blood money, in quasi-deliberate killing, and in pure killing by error.

Know that the majority agree that the blood money for pure deliberate killing and quasi-deliberate killing is the same, but they differ on its age categories for both. A group of the people of knowledge held that it is in four equal parts: twenty-five bint makhad (a female camel in its second year), twenty-five bint labun (a female camel in its third year), twenty-five hiqqah (a female camel in its fourth year), and twenty-five jadha'ah (a female camel in its fifth year).

This is the view of Malik and Abu Hanifah, the well-known narration from Ahmad, and the saying of al-Zuhri, Rabi'ah, and Sulayman ibn Yasar. It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud, as Ibn Qudamah transmitted it from them in al-Mughni.

Another group held that it is thirty hiqqah, thirty jadha'ah, and forty pregnant she-camels with their young in their wombs.

This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and it was said by 'Ata', Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and it was reported from 'Umar, Zayd, Abu Musa, and al-Mughirah. A group also narrated it from Imam Ahmad.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, said: This view is the one which the evidence indicates as stronger, because of what was previously mentioned in the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As in Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Of them, forty are pregnant she-camels with their young in their wombs." Some of its chains are sound, as was previously mentioned.

Al-Bayhaqi, in explaining the sixty which this hadith did not specify, said: "Chapter on the description of the sixty which accompany the forty," and then cited his chains from 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and 'Ali (in one of his two narrations from him) that they are thirty hiqqah and thirty jadha'ah.

Ibn Qudamah in al-Mughni, citing evidence for this view, said: "Its evidence is what 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb narrated, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever kills deliberately, he is handed over to the heirs of the victim. If they wish, they may kill him, and if they wish, they may take the blood money, which is thirty hiqqah, thirty jadha'ah, and forty khilfah (pregnant she-camels). Whatever they agree upon is theirs.' This is because of the severity of killing." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: "It is a hasan gharib hadith." (End of quotation, the relevant part in its wording.) Then he cited the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As which we mentioned previously.

Then he said, citing evidence for the first view: "The basis of the first view is what al-Zuhri narrated from al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, who said: 'The blood money in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in four parts: twenty-five jadha'ah, twenty-five hiqqah, twenty-five bint labun, and twenty-five bint makhad.' This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud." (End of his quotation.)

In the Muwatta' of Malik: that Ibn Shihab used to say regarding the blood money for deliberate killing when it is accepted: twenty-five bint makhad, twenty-five bint labun, twenty-five hiqqah, and twenty-five jadha'ah. We have already mentioned that the blood money for deliberate killing and the blood money for quasi-deliberate killing are the same according to the majority.

Regarding the blood money for quasi-deliberate killing, the scholars have views other than those we have mentioned. Among them is what al-Bayhaqi and Abu Dawud narrated from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "For quasi-deliberate killing, there are three thirds: thirty-three hiqqah, thirty-three jadha'ah, and thirty-four thaniyyah (a female camel in its sixth year) up to the beginning of its ninth year (bazil), and all of them are khilfah."

Among them is also what al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud as well: that they are in quarters: a quarter bint labun, a quarter hiqaq (plural of hiqqah), a quarter jidha' (plural of jadha'ah), and a quarter thaniyyah up to the bazil of its year. This is the summary of the views of the people of knowledge regarding the blood money for deliberate killing and quasi-deliberate killing.

The most preferred and strongest of these views is what the Sunnah indicates, which is what we mentioned: thirty hiqqah, thirty jadha'ah, and forty pregnant she-camels with their young in their wombs.

Al-Bayhaqi (may Allah have mercy on him) said in al-Sunan al-Kubra, after citing the views mentioned, the following: "They have differed in this manner, and the view of the one who agrees with the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in the chapter before it is more worthy of being followed. And success is from Allah."

Note (tanbih)

Know that the blood money for pure deliberate killing, when the victim's heirs pardon, is only from the property of the perpetrator, and the 'aqilah does not bear it, by consensus. The more apparent of the two views is that it is due in full at once and not spread out over years, and this is the view of the majority of the people of knowledge. It was said that it is paid in installments (tanjim).

According to Abu Hanifah, there is no fixed blood money at all for deliberate killing. Rather, what is obligatory in it is whatever the perpetrator and the victim's heirs agree upon, whether little or much, and it is due immediately according to him.

As for the blood money for quasi-deliberate killing, it is paid in installments over three years, a third of it being paid at the end of each of the three years, and the beginning of the year is reckoned from the time the blood money becomes due.

Some of the people of knowledge said: its beginning is from the time the judge rules for the blood money, and it is borne by the 'aqilah, because of what we mentioned in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, agreed upon (in al-Bukhari and Muslim), that it is borne by the 'aqilah. This is the view of the three Imams: Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on them all). It was also said by al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Hakam, al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others, as Ibn Qudamah, the author of al-Mughni, transmitted from them. And this view is the truth.

Some of the people of knowledge held that the blood money for quasi-deliberate killing is from the property of the perpetrator and not from the 'aqilah, because he intended the striking, even though he did not intend the killing. This was said by Ibn Sirin, al-Zuhri, al-Harith al-'Ukli, Ibn Shubrumah, Qatadah, Abu Thawr, and Abu Bakr 'Abd al-'Aziz chose it. (End of quotation from Ibn Qudamah's al-Mughni.) You have learned that the correct position is the opposite of this, because of the indication of the hadith agreed upon on this point.

As for Malik (may Allah have mercy on him), he does not hold the concept of quasi-deliberate killing at all; for him, it is pure deliberate killing, as was previously mentioned.

As for the blood money for pure killing by error, according to the view of most of the people of knowledge, it is in five categories.

Most of them agreed on the age and type for four of them and differed about the fifth. The four on which most agree are: twenty jadha'ah, twenty hiqqah, twenty bint labun, and twenty bint makhad. As for the fifth, about which there is disagreement, some of the people of knowledge say it is twenty ibn makhad, male, which is the view of Ahmad and Abu Hanifah, and it was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, and Ibn al-Mundhir. The proponents of this view relied on the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud concerning it.

Abu Dawud said in his Sunan: Musaddad narrated to us, 'Abd al-Wahid narrated to us, al-Hajjaj narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Jubayr, from Khashf ibn Malik al-Ta'i, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For the blood money of error: twenty hiqqah, twenty jadha'ah, twenty bint makhad, twenty bint labun, and twenty ibn makhad male." This is the view of 'Abdullah. (End of his quotation, in his wording.)

Al-Nasa'i said in his Sunan: 'Ali ibn Sa'id ibn Masruq informed us, saying: Yahya ibn Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'idah narrated to us, from al-Hajjaj, from Zayd ibn Jubayr, from Khashf ibn Malik al-Ta'i, who said: "I heard Ibn Mas'ud say: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decreed the blood money for error as twenty bint makhad, twenty ibn makhad males, twenty bint labun, twenty jadha'ah, and twenty hiqqah.'"

Ibn Majah said in his Sunan: 'Abd al-Salam ibn 'Asim narrated to us, al-Sabbah ibn Muharib narrated to us, al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah narrated to us, Zayd ibn Jubayr narrated to us, from Khashf ibn Malik al-Ta'i, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For the blood money of error: twenty hiqqah, twenty jadha'ah, twenty bint makhad, twenty bint labun, and twenty banu makhad males." A similar report was also recorded by al-Tirmidhi from Ibn Mas'ud.

Al-Daraqutni also recorded a similar report from him, except that in it is "twenty banu labun" instead of "banu makhad."

Al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) said in Bulugh al-Maram: "Its chain is stronger than the chain of the four (collections)." He said: "Ibn Abi Shaybah also recorded it through another route, as a mawquf (ending with a Companion), and it is more sound than the marfu' (ascribed to the Prophet)."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 33 (part 5 of 7):

As for the second opinion regarding this disputed fifth category, it is that the diya is twenty ibn labun males (male camels in their third year), together with twenty jadha'ah (camels in their fifth year), twenty hiqqah (camels in their fourth year), twenty bint labun (female camels in their third year), and twenty bint makhad (female camels in their second year). This is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Sulayman ibn Yasar, al-Zuhri, al-Layth, and Rabi'ah also held it. Ibn Qudamah transmitted it from them in *al-Mughni*, and said: "Thus did Sa'id narrate it in his *Sunan*, from al-Nakha'i, from Ibn Mas'ud."

Al-Khattabi said: It has been related that "the Prophet ﷺ paid the blood money for the man who was killed at Khaybar with one hundred camels from the sadaqah (zakat camels)," and there is no ibn makhad among the age categories of sadaqah.

Al-Bayhaqi said in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Raffa' al-Baghdadi informed us, Abu 'Amr 'Uthman ibn Muhammad ibn Bishr informed us, Isma'il ibn Ishaq al-Qadi related to us, Isma'il ibn Abi Uways and 'Isa ibn Mina related to us, both saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Zinad related to us, that his father said: "Among our jurists whose opinions were relied upon were Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, Kharijah ibn Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah, and Sulayman ibn Yasar, along with a great company of their peers. When they differed on a matter, we followed the view of the majority of them and the most excellent of them in judgment. They used to say: The 'aql (blood money) for accidental killing is five fifths: one fifth jidha', one fifth hiqaq, one fifth bint labun, one fifth bint makhad, and one fifth ibn labun males. And the tooth (compensation) for every wound, whether small or great, is five fifths in this same description." End of al-Bayhaqi's words, may Allah have mercy on him.

The one who wrote this, may Allah pardon him, says: Some scholars held that the stronger of the two opinions in evidence is the view of those who said that the fifth category consists of the male sons of the makhad, not of the sons of the labun, based on the marfu' hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn (p-107) Mas'ud, which explicitly states the Prophet ﷺ's judgment in this matter. They said: Although the hadith in question has its problems, it is preferable to adopting other opinion over it.

As for the chain of Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, all its narrators are fit to be used as evidence, except al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah, for there is much discussion about him and disagreement among the scholars. Some consider him trustworthy, and some consider him weak. We have already mentioned in this blessed book the weakening of him by some of the scholars.

Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Truthful, but he makes many errors and practices tadlis (concealment of defects in narration)."

The one who wrote this, may Allah pardon him, says: The aforementioned al-Hajjaj is one of the narrators of Muslim. Abu Dawud, al-Bayhaqi, and others gave the hadith a defect (i'lal) by holding it to be mawquf (ending with Ibn Mas'ud), saying that its attribution as marfu' to the Prophet ﷺ is an error. We have already pointed to this shortly before.

As for the reliability of the remaining narrators of the Sunan: In Abu Dawud's chain, the first tabaqah (level) is Musaddad, who is a trustworthy and retentive (hafiz) narrator. In al-Nasa'i's chain, it is Sa'id ibn 'Ali ibn Sa'id ibn Masruq al-Kindi al-Kufi, who is truthful.

The second tabaqah in Abu Dawud's chain is 'Abd al-Wahid, who is Ibn Ziyad al-'Abdi, their mawla (client), the Basran, who is trustworthy, though there is criticism regarding his narrations from al-A'mash alone. In al-Nasa'i's chain it is Yahya ibn Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'idah, who is trustworthy and precise.

The third tabaqah in both chains is al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah, mentioned above.

The fourth tabaqah in both is Zayd ibn Jubayr, who is trustworthy.

The fifth tabaqah in both is Khashf ibn Malik al-Ta'i, whom al-Nasa'i declared trustworthy.

The sixth tabaqah in both is 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ.

The first tabaqah in Ibn Majah's chain is 'Abd al-Salam ibn 'Asim al-Ju'fi al-Hisinjani al-Razi, who is acceptable (maqbul).

The second tabaqah in his chain is al-Sabbah ibn Muharib al-Taymi al-Kufi, a resident of al-Rayy, who is truthful but sometimes opposes others (in narration).

The third tabaqah in his chain is al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah, down to the end of the mentioned chain.

The summary: The hadith is criticized from two angles. The first is due to al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah, whom most scholars have weakened, though some have declared him trustworthy, and he is one of the narrators of Muslim. The second is its being given the defect of being mawquf. As for what al-Khattabi used as evidence, namely that "the Prophet ﷺ paid for the one killed at Khaybar with camels from sadaqah, and there is no ibn makhad among the ages of sadaqah camels," it may be said in response that the one killed at Khaybar was killed intentionally, whereas our discussion concerns accidental killing. As for the argument of those who say that the sons of the labun should replace the sons of the makhad, it rests on the marfu' narration of al-Daraqutni, of which Ibn Hajar said its chain is more authentic than the narration of the sons of the makhad, and on the large number of scholars who held this view.

There are other opinions among the scholars regarding the diya for accidental killing besides those we have mentioned, and they supported them with other hadiths. Consult them in the *Sunan* of al-Nasa'i, Abu Dawud, al-Bayhaqi, and others.

Know that the diya is, on the people of gold, one thousand dinars, and on the people of silver (warq), twelve thousand dirhams, according to the majority (jumhur).

Abu Hanifah said: ten thousand dirhams. On the people of cattle, two hundred cows; on the people of sheep, two thousand sheep; and on the people of garments (hulal), two hundred garments.

Abu Dawud said in his *Sunan*: Yahya ibn Hakim related to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Uthman related to us, Husayn al-Mu'allim related to us, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "The value of the diya in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was eight hundred dinars, or eight thousand dirhams, and the diya of the People of the Book on that day was half the diya of the Muslims."

He said: "So it remained thus, until 'Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, was made caliph. He stood and gave a sermon, saying: 'Behold, camels have become expensive.' So he set it on the people of gold at one thousand dinars, on the people of silver at twelve thousand, on the people of cattle at two hundred cows, on the people of sheep at two thousand sheep, and on the people of garments at two hundred garments, and he left the diya of the People of the Book unchanged from what he raised of the diya."

Musa ibn Isma'il related to us, Hammad related to us, Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "judged for the diya on the people of camels: one hundred camels; on the people of cattle: two hundred cows; on the people of sheep: two thousand sheep; on the people of garments: two hundred garments; and on the people of wheat: something which Muhammad did not remember."

Abu Dawud said: I read to Sa'id ibn Ya'qub al-Talaqani, who said: Abu Tumaylah related to us, Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: 'Ata' mentioned, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set..." (p-109) and he mentioned a similar hadith to that of Musa, and said: "And on the people of food, something which I do not remember."

Al-Nasa'i said in his *Sunan*: Ahmad ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Rashid informed us, from Sulayman ibn Musa, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever is killed by accident, his diya is one hundred camels: thirty bint makhad, thirty bint labun, thirty hiqqah, and ten ibn labun males."

He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to assess it on the people of the villages at four hundred dinars, or its equivalent in silver. He assessed it on the people of camels, and when camels became expensive he raised its value, and when they became cheap he reduced its value according to the times as they were. So its value in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ranged between four hundred dinars and eight hundred dinars, or its equivalent in silver."

He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ decreed that whoever's 'aql was in cattle, then on the people of cattle, two hundred cows; and whoever's 'aql was in sheep, two thousand sheep. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ decreed that the 'aql is an inheritance among the heirs of the slain according to their shares, and whatever remains goes to the 'asabah (male agnatic relatives). And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ decreed that the woman's 'aql is borne by her 'asabah, whoever they may be, and they do not inherit from it except what remains after her heirs, and if she is killed, her 'aql is among her heirs, and they are the ones who take retaliation against her killer."

Al-Nasa'i said in his *Sunan*: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna informed us, from Mu'adh ibn Hani', who said: Muhammad ibn Muslim related to me, from 'Amr ibn Dinar (ḥ), and Abu Dawud informed us, saying: Mu'adh ibn Hani' related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Muslim related to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man killed a man in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so the Prophet ﷺ made his diya twelve thousand, and he mentioned the statement of Allah: ﴿Except that Allah and His Messenger enriched them out of His bounty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74], regarding their taking of the diya." The wording is that of Abu Dawud: Muhammad ibn Maymun informed us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from 'Amr, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas:

That the Prophet ﷺ "decided on twelve thousand," meaning for the diya. End of al-Nasa'i's words, may Allah have mercy on him.

Abu Dawud also said in his *Sunan*: Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Anbari related to us, Zayd ibn al-Hubab related to us, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "A man from the Banu 'Adi was killed, so the Prophet ﷺ made his diya twelve thousand." Abu Dawud said: Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated it from 'Amr, from 'Ikrimah, from the Prophet ﷺ, and did not mention Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Majah said in his *Sunan*: al-'Abbas ibn Ja'far related to us, Muhammad ibn Sinan related to us, (p-110) Muhammad ibn Muslim related to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, "from the Prophet ﷺ: 'He made the diya twelve thousand.'" He said: And that is the meaning of His statement: ﴿And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger enriched them out of His bounty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74]. He said: by their taking of the diya.

In the *Muwatta'* from Malik: It reached him that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab assessed the diya on the people of the villages, making it on the people of gold one thousand dinars, and on the people of silver twelve thousand dirhams. Malik said: The people of gold are the people of Syria and Egypt, and the people of silver are the people of Iraq.

Also from Malik in the *Muwatta'*: He heard that the diya is paid in three years or four years. Malik said: Three years is the most preferred of what I have heard regarding that.

Malik said: The matter agreed upon among us is that from the people of the villages, camels are not accepted as diya, nor are gold or silver from the people of the 'amud (a traditional unit of value), nor is silver accepted from the people of gold, nor gold from the people of silver.

* *

Branches related to this issue.

The first: The majority of scholars hold that the diya for accidental killing and quasi-intentional killing is deferred over three years, paid as one third in each of the three years.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: There is no disagreement among them that it is deferred over three years, for 'Umar and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, made the diya for accidental killing binding on the 'aqilah over three years, and we know of no opponent of them among the Companions, so the scholars followed them in this. End quote.

The one who wrote this, may Allah pardon him, says: Such a matter is called a silent consensus (ijma' sukuti), and it is a presumptive proof according to a group of the scholars of usul al-fiqh. The author of *Maraqi al-Su'ud* pointed to this, together with the condition for relying on it according to those who hold this view, in his words:

Making the one who keeps silent like the one who affirms is well known to have a disagreement among them.
So relying on the silent consensus has been a matter of debate among those who came before.
It is most fitting when there is no displeasure and no opposite, with the passing of a period for consideration.

And deferring it over three years is the view of most of the scholars.

* *

The second branch: The scholars differ regarding the perpetrator himself: whether he is obligated to bear a share of the diya for accidental killing, like one of the 'aqilah, or not.

The position of Abu Hanifah and the well-known position of Malik is that the perpetrator is obligated to bear a share of the diya, like one member of the 'aqilah.

Al-Imam Ahmad and al-Shafi'i went to the view that he is not obligated to pay any of the diya, based on the apparent meaning of the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, agreed upon, previously mentioned: "The Prophet ﷺ decided the diya for the 'aqilah of the woman," and its apparent meaning is that he decided the entire diya is upon the 'aqilah. The argument of the other view is that the origin of the offence is upon him, and they (the 'aqilah) are helping him, so he bears for himself an amount similar to what a man from his 'aqilah bears.

* *

**Section Three:** The scholars differed over identifying the ʿāqila (the group of kin who bear the blood money on behalf of the perpetrator) that shares the payment of accidental killing (diyat al-khaṭaʾ).

The position of Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the ʿāqila are the people of the perpetrator's dīwān (the military register), if the perpetrator is one of the people of a dīwān. The people of the dīwān are the people of the banners, namely the army whose names are written in the dīwān so that they support one another. The diya is taken from their stipends over three years.
