If the perpetrator is not one of the people of a dīwān, then his ʿāqila is his tribe, and the diya is divided among them over three years. If the tribe cannot bear it, the nearest tribes in lineage are added to them, following the order of the ʿaṣaba (agnatic kin).

The position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is likewise to begin with the people of the dīwān. The diya is taken from their stipends over three years. If they have no current stipend, then his ʿāqila is his ʿaṣaba, the nearest and then the next nearest. Women and children do not bear any part of the ʿaql (blood money).

There is no fixed limit to the wealth of the ʿāqila, such that once they reach it they bear the diya, nor is there a fixed limit to what is taken from them. Their wealthy are not required to pay on behalf of their poor.

Whoever has no ʿaṣaba, his ʿaql is paid from the Treasury of the Muslims (bayt al-māl).

The mawālī (clients) hold the same position as the ʿaṣaba among the relatives. The son and the father are included among the relatives.

Saḥnūn said: If the ʿāqila number a thousand, they are few, and the nearest tribes to them are added.

The position of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is that no individual member of the ʿaṣaba may be made to pay more than one dirham and a third per year over the three years, so that the total is four dirhams.

The position of Ahmad and al-Shafiʿi is that the people of the dīwān have no share in the ʿaql unless they are ʿaṣaba. Their position, may Allah have mercy on both of them, is that the ʿāqila are the ʿaṣaba. However, they differed over whether fathers and sons are included in that. Ahmad, in one of the two reports from him, holds that they are included among the ʿaṣaba, because they are the nearest of the ʿaṣaba. Another report from Ahmad, and al-Shafiʿi, holds that they are not included in the ʿāqila, because of the apparent meaning of the hadith of Abu Hurayra, agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh), mentioned earlier: "The inheritance of a woman goes to her children, and the diya is upon her ʿāqila." [p-112] Its apparent meaning excludes her children, so the fathers are analogized to the children.

Ibn Qudama said in al-Mughni: The people of knowledge differed over what each individual among them bears.

Ahmad said: They bear according to what they are able to bear. This is not fixed by the Sharia; rather, it is left to the judgment (ijtihād) of the ruler, who imposes on each person an amount that is easy and does not cause harm. This is also the position of Malik, because a fixed measure is established only by revelatory stipulation (tawqīf), and is not established by opinion or arbitrary decision. There is no text on this matter, so it must be left to the ruler's judgment, like the measures of maintenance expenses.

A second report from Ahmad is that the wealthy person is required to pay half a mithqal, because that is the smallest amount of wealth that has a fixed measure in zakat, so it is taken as the standard. The middling person is required to pay a quarter of a mithqal, because anything less than that is trivial, since the hand is not cut for it. ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The hand is not cut for a trivial thing, and the hand is not cut for less than a quarter of a dinar." This is the choice of Abu Bakr, and the position of al-Shafiʿi.

Abu Hanifa said: The most that is borne by one person is four dirhams, and there is no minimum for the least amount. End of the words of the author of al-Mughni.

* *

**Section Four:** The ʿāqila do not bear any part of the expiation (kaffāra) mentioned in His saying: ﴿and freeing a believing slave﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 92]. Rather, it is due from the wealth of the perpetrator, by consensus. Whoever said it is due from the Treasury (bayt al-māl) is an outlier.

Expiation for accidental killing is obligatory by consensus, based on the explicit noble verse concerning that.

They differed concerning deliberate killing, and their difference on it is well known. In my view, the more consistent of the two positions by analogy is the view of those who say there is no expiation for deliberate killing, because the gravity of deliberate killing is greater than that it could be expiated by freeing a slave. This is based on His saying, concerning the one who kills deliberately: ﴿But his recompense is Hell, abiding therein; and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 93]. This matter is too high and too grave to be expiated by freeing a slave. And Allah knows best.

The ʿāqila do not bear the diya if the killing was accidental and is established by the confession of the perpetrator and they did not confirm it. Rather, they bear it only if the killing is established by evidence (bayyina). This is what the majority of the people of knowledge held, including Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shaʿbi, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Sulayman ibn Musa, al-Thawri, [p-113] al-Awzaʿi and Ishaq. It is also the position of al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Malik, Abu Hanifa and others. And Allah knows best.

* *

**Section Five:** The majority of scholars hold that the diya of a free Muslim woman is half the diya of a free Muslim man, as we have explained.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: The people of knowledge agreed that the diya of a woman is half the diya of a man. Others have reported from Ibn ʿUlayya and al-Asamm that they said her diya is like the diya of a man. This is an anomalous view, contrary to the consensus of the Companions, as stated by the author of al-Mughni.

The wounds (jirāḥ) of a woman are equal to the wounds of a man up to a third of the diya; if they reach a third, then it is half. Ibn Qudama said in al-Mughni: This is reported from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿUmar and Zayd ibn Thabit, and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Zuhri, Qatada, al-Aʿraj, Rabiʿa and Malik also held it.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: This is the view of the seven jurists of Medina and the majority of the people of Medina, and it is reported from al-Shafiʿi in his earlier (qadīm) view.

Al-Hasan said: They are equal up to half. It is reported from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that her diya is half of his in both small and large amounts. This was also reported from Ibn Sirin, and it was held by al-Thawri, al-Layth, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Shubruma, Abu Hanifa and his companions, Abu Thawr, and al-Shafiʿi in the apparent (ẓāhir) of his school. Ibn al-Mundhir chose it, because they are two persons whose diya differs, so the compensation (arsh) for their wounds differs. End of quotation. This view is more analogous.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: The words of Ibn Qudama and al-Khiraqi are explicit that what reaches a third of the diya is equal for both of them, and that her being given half the diya over him applies only to what exceeds a third. Thus the implication of their words is that the diya for a woman's jāʾifa (a wound penetrating to the body cavity) and maʾmūma (a head wound reaching the skull) is like the diya for a man's jāʾifa and maʾmūma, because each of the jāʾifa and the maʾmūma carries a third of the diya. Her ʿaql is not half of his except for what exceeds a third, like the diya for four fingers of the hand, for in them are forty camels, since each finger has ten, and forty is more than a third of a hundred. The words of Malik in al-Muwatta and elsewhere are explicit that for what reaches a third, like the jāʾifa and maʾmūma, a woman's diya is half a man's, and that the place where they are equal is only for what is less than a third, such as the mūdiḥa (a wound that exposes the bone), the munaqqila (a wound that causes bone displacement), and one, two or three fingers. These are two well-known views among the people of knowledge, and the more correct of them is what we have mentioned from Malik, which Ibn Qudama preferred at the end of his discussion, with the hadith that will come, Allah willing.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: This view is extremely problematic, because it implies that if a woman cuts three fingers from her hand, her diya is thirty camels like a man's fingers, since it is less than a third; but if she cuts four fingers from her hand, her diya is twenty camels, because it exceeds a third, so it becomes half a man's diya. That the diya for three fingers is thirty camels and the diya for four fingers is twenty is extremely problematic, as you can see.

Rabiʿa ibn Abi ʿAbd al-Rahman raised this problem with Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, and he answered that this is the Sunna. In the Muwatta of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, from Malik, from Rabiʿa ibn Abi ʿAbd al-Rahman, he said: I asked Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab: How much is due for a woman's finger? He said: Ten camels. I said: How much for two fingers? He said: Twenty camels. I said: How much for three? He said: Thirty camels. I said: How much for four? He said: Twenty camels. I said: When her wound becomes great and her affliction intensifies, her ʿaql decreases? Saʿid said: Are you an Iraqi? I said: Rather, I am a scholar who is careful, or an ignorant one who is seeking to learn. Saʿid said: It is the Sunna, my nephew.

The apparent meaning of Saʿid's words is that this is from the Sunna of the Prophet (ﷺ). If we say that this has the ruling of a marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet) report, it is still a mursal (a report whose chain omits a Companion), because Saʿid did not meet the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). The discussion of the mursal reports of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab has already been treated fully in the commentary on Surat al-Anʿam. Moreover, some scholars said that by "Sunna" he means here the Sunna of the people of Medina.

Al-Nasaʾi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sunan: Isa ibn Yunus informed us, saying: Hamza narrated to us from Ismaʿil ibn ʿAyyash, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The ʿaql of a woman is like the ʿaql of a man until it reaches a third of her diya." End of quotation. This supports the words of Saʿid that this is the Sunna.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: The chain of this report of al-Nasaʾi is apparently weak for two reasons.

The first: Ismaʿil ibn ʿAyyash narrated it from Ibn Jurayj, and Ismaʿil's narrations from non-Syrians are weak, as we have already explained. Ibn Jurayj is not a Syrian; rather, he is a Hijazi Meccan.

[p-115] The second: Ibn Jurayj reported it with the ʿanʿana formula ("from") from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, and Ibn Jurayj, may Allah have mercy on him, is a mudallis (one who conceals defects in his chain). The ʿanʿana of a mudallis is not accepted as evidence unless the hearing (samāʿ) is established through another route, as is established in the sciences of hadith. This flaw is supported by what al-Tirmidhi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: that Muhammad ibn Ismaʿil, meaning al-Bukhari, said that Ibn Jurayj did not hear from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. Ibn Hajar transmitted this from him in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib in the biography of the aforementioned Ibn Jurayj.

From what we have mentioned, you know that Ibn Khuzayma's authentication of this hadith is not sound, even though Ibn Hajar transmitted it from him in Bulugh al-Maram and remained silent about it. And Allah knows best. Along with what preceded, this hadith's content would necessarily mean that there are thirty camels for three of a woman's fingers and twenty for four of her fingers, which contradicts the wisdom of this noble Sharia that is known, as you can see. Unless it is said that if the woman is placed at half of the man for what reaches a third and beyond, this applies only to the excess, so that for four of her fingers there are thirty-five camels, and the reduction falls only on the fourth finger. This is reasonable and apparent, and the hadith admits of this interpretation. And Allah knows best.

Among the evidences that a woman's diya is half a man's diya is what al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Sunan al-Kubra by two routes from ʿUbada ibn Nusayy, from Ibn Ghanam, from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The diya of a woman is half the diya of a man." Then al-Bayhaqi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It was also narrated by another route from ʿUbada ibn Nusayy, and in it there is weakness. It is known that ʿUbada ibn Nusayy is trustworthy and excellent, so the weakness al-Bayhaqi meant is from someone other than him. Al-Bayhaqi also narrated from ʿAli, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The diya of a woman is half the diya of a man in all cases." This is from the narration of Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi from him, and it has a break in its chain (inqiṭaʿ). Ibn Abi Shayba narrated it through al-Shaʿbi from him, and he also narrated it by another route from him and from ʿUmar. This was said by al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him.

* *

**The Sixth Branch:** Know that the most sound and clearest of the opinions in evidence is that the blood money (*diyya*) of a non-Muslim subject (*dhimmi*) is half the blood money of a Muslim, as we mentioned earlier from Abu Dawud, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The blood money of the People of the Book, in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was half the blood money of the Muslims." And [it is also established] that Umar, when he revised the blood money because camels had become expensive, did not raise it for them along with what he raised.

Abu Dawud also said in his *Sunan*: Yazid ibn Khalid ibn Mawhab al-Ramli narrated to us, Isa ibn Yunus narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The blood money of the one under covenant (*mu'ahid*) is half the blood money of a free man." Abu Dawud said: It was also narrated by Usama ibn Zayd al-Laythi (p-116) and Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, in the same manner. End.

Al-Nasa'i said in his *Sunan*: Amr ibn Ali narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Rashid narrated to us, from Sulayman ibn Musa... (and he mentioned a word whose meaning is [the same]) from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The blood money (*aql*) of the People of the Dhimma is half the blood money of the Muslims, and they are the Jews and the Christians." Ahmad ibn Amr ibn al-Sarh informed us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Usama ibn Zayd informed me, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Amr, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The blood money of the disbeliever is half the blood money of the believer."

Ibn Majah, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his *Sunan*: Hisham ibn Ammar narrated to us, Hatim ibn Isma'il narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ayyash, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "decreed that the blood money of the People of the Two Books is half the blood money of the Muslims, and they are the Jews and the Christians." Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi also narrated something similar, from Amr, from his father, from his grandfather.

Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: This hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb was graded *hasan* by al-Tirmidhi, and declared *sahih* by Ibn al-Jarud. From this you know that this view is preferable to the view of those who said: the blood money of the People of the Dhimma is like the blood money of the Muslims, such as Abu Hanifa and those who agree with him; and to the view of those who said: it is a third of the blood money of a Muslim, such as al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him. And Allah knows best.

Know that the narrations which state that the blood money of the *dhimmi* and the *mu'ahid* is like that of a Muslim are weak and cannot be used as evidence. Al-Bayhaqi, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, has shown their weakness in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*. Ibn al-Turkumani, may Allah have mercy on him, attempted in his commentary on the *Sunan* of al-Bayhaqi to make those narrations suitable for use as evidence, but there is nothing sound in them.

As for using the apparent meaning of Allah's words, ﴿and a compensation paid to his family﴾ [al-Nisa: 92], it is said in reply: this is an inference by juxtaposition (*dalalat al-iqtiran*), which is not considered valid by the majority of scholars. The most that can be said is that the verse does not specify the amount of the blood money of a Muslim or of a disbeliever, while the Sunna has made clear that the blood money of the disbeliever is half the blood money of the Muslim, and this is not problematic.

As for their equality in the amount of expiation (*kaffara*), there is no evidence in it concerning blood money, because that is a separate question.

The evidences we have mentioned, whose indication is that it is half the blood money of a Muslim, are stronger. It is also supported by the document which the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote for Amr ibn Hazm: "And for a believing soul (*nafs mu'mina*), a hundred camels." The implication (*mafhum*) of the word "believing" is that a disbelieving soul is not so. Moreover, the one who opposes this is Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is established in his principles that the indication by contrast (*dalil al-khitab*), I mean the implication of contrary meaning (*mafhum al-mukhalafa*), is not considered valid, as is well known from him. And he does not hold to restricting the absolute (*haml al-mutlaq ala al-muqayyad*), so he would not use the unqualified word "soul" (*nafs*), free from the condition of faith, in other evidences as proof that it includes the disbeliever. Nor do we know of any basis in the Book or the Sunna for the view that distinguishes between a disbeliever killed intentionally, whose blood money is then like that of a Muslim, and one killed by mistake, whose blood money is then half that of a Muslim. And Allah knows best.

As for the blood money of the Magian (*majusi*): most scholars hold that it is one-third of one-fifth of the blood money of a Muslim, which is eight hundred dirhams, and their women are half of that.

This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and most scholars; among them Umar, Uthman, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Ata', Ikrima, al-Hasan, and Ishaq.

It is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that he said: his blood money is half the blood money of a Muslim, like the blood money of a People of the Book.

Al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi said: his blood money is like the blood money of a Muslim, and this is the school of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him.

The use of the hadith "Treat them according to the sunna of the People of the Book" as evidence that the blood money of the Magian is like that of the People of the Book is not valid, because even if we assume the hadith is fit for use as evidence, what is meant by it is only taking the *jizya* from them, as evidenced by the fact that their women are not lawful [to marry] and their slaughtered animals are not lawful to eat. End.

Ibn Qudama said in *al-Mughni*: the view of those Companions we have mentioned, that the blood money of the Magian is one-third of one-fifth of the blood money of a Muslim, was not opposed by any of the Companions, so it became a tacit consensus (*ijma' sukuti*). We have already mentioned the view of those who said it is a binding proof.

Some scholars said: the blood money of an apostate (*murtadd*), if he is killed before being asked to repent (*istitaba*), is like the blood money of a Magian; and this is the school of Malik. As for those at war (*harbiyyun*), they have no blood money whatsoever. And Allah knows best.

[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 36 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart – about all of those one will be questioned.﴾

In this noble verse, exalted is He forbids a person from following what he has no knowledge of. This includes his saying: "I saw," when he did not see; "I heard," when he did not hear; "I knew," when he did not know. It also includes every statement made without knowledge, and a person acting on what he does not know. Exalted is He has indicated this meaning in other verses, such as His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality, and to say about Allah that which you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169], and His saying:
﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has not sent down authority, and that you say about Allah that which you do not know﴾ [al-A'raf: 33], and His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of [the] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12] – the verse – 
• and His saying: ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent [lies] against Allah?﴾ [Yunus: 59],
• and His saying: ﴿And indeed, assumption avails not against the truth at all﴾ [al-Najm: 28],
• and His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of it; they follow only assumption﴾ [al-Nisa': 157],
and the verses of this kind, in condemnation of following other than knowledge, which is forbidden in this noble verse, are very numerous. And in a hadith: "Beware of assumption, for assumption is the most false of speech."
* *
NOTE
Some scholars took from this noble verse the prohibition of taqlid (blind following), saying: because it is following what is not knowledge.
Its commentator, may Allah pardon him, says: There is no doubt that blind taqlid, for which Allah condemned the disbelievers in verses of His Book, this verse and others like it indicate its prohibition, and the disbelief of the one who follows it;
• such as His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow that upon which we found our fathers." Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 104]
• and His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is that upon which we found our fathers." Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 104],
• and His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow that upon which we found our fathers." Even if Satan was inviting them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾ [Luqman: 21],
• and His saying: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so they are holding to it? Rather, they say, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed, we are guided by their footsteps."﴾ ﴿And likewise, We did not send before you any warner into a city except that its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed, we are following in their footsteps."﴾ ﴿[The warner] said, "Even if I brought you better guidance than that upon which you found your fathers?"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 24],
• and His saying: ﴿They said, "You are not but a human being like us, who wants to avert us from that which our fathers used to worship"﴾ – the verse – [Ibrahim: 10],
and to other verses besides these.
* *
As for the argument of some of the Zahiriyyah, such as Ibn Hazm and those who followed him, using this verse under discussion and similar verses to prohibit ijtihad in the Sharia absolutely, and to declare misguided the one who holds it, and to prohibit taqlid altogether – this is placing the Qur'an in other than its proper place and interpreting it contrary to its meaning, as is common among the Zahiriyyah; because the legitimacy of the ignorant person asking the scholar and acting on his fatwa is a matter known from the religion by necessity, and it is known that the common person used to ask some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and they would give him a fatwa, and he would act upon their fatwa, and none of the Muslims denied that. Just as it is known that if a matter has no text in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ, then the scholar's ijtihad, to the extent of his capacity, in understanding the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ, to know the ruling of what is silent about from what is stated, has no basis for prohibition, and it was practiced among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and none of the Muslims denied it. We will clarify in full detail, if Allah the Exalted wills, in "Surat al-Anbiya' and al-Hashr," the matter of ijtihad in the Sharia, and the deduction of the ruling of what is silent about from what is stated by attaching it to it, whether by qiyas or otherwise, and we will explain the evidences for that, and clarify the refutation of the doubts of those who oppose, such as the Zahiriyyah and al-Nazzam, and whoever says their saying, in their argument with hadiths and verses of the Book of Allah for their claim, and with rational doubts, until the invalidity of all that becomes clear.
* *
We will mention here a small portion of that by which the validity of saying ijtihad and qiyas in what has no text is known, and that attaching the like to its textually stated counterpart is not contrary to the noble Sharia.
Know first that attaching what is silent about to what is stated, by negating the distinguishing factor between them, is hardly denied except by the obstinate; and it is a type of clear qiyas, which al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, calls "qiyas in the meaning of the original" (al-qiyas fi ma'na al-asl), and most jurists of usul do not apply the name qiyas to it, although it is attaching what is silent about to what is stated because there is no difference between them; I mean the difference that affects the ruling.
Among the examples of this type is His saying: ﴿So do not say to them, "uff"﴾ [al-Isra': 23]; for no sensible person doubts that the prohibition of saying "uff," which is stated, indicates the prohibition of striking, which is silent about.
And His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7, 8]; there is also no doubt that the explicit statement of accountability for the weight of an atom and reward for it, which is stated, indicates accountability and reward for the weight of a mountain, which is silent about.
And His saying: ﴿And bring to witness two just men from among you﴾ – the verse – [al-Talaq: 2]; there is no doubt that it indicates that the testimony of four just men is accepted, although the testimony of four is silent about.
And his saying, peace be upon him, prohibiting sacrifice with a one-eyed animal indicates the prohibition of sacrificing with a blind animal, although that is silent about.
And His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans﴾ – the verse – [al-Nisa': 10]; there is no doubt that it indicates the prohibition of burning or drowning the orphan's property, because all of that is destruction of it without right.
And his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever frees his share in a slave, and he has wealth that reaches the price of the slave, he is valued against him at the fair value, and his partners are given their shares, and the slave is freed by him; otherwise, what he freed of him is freed." This indicates that whoever frees his share in a female slave, her ruling is likewise, because of what is known from the inductive study of the Sharia that maleness and femaleness, in relation to manumission, are incidental attributes (tardiyyan) that have no effect on the rulings of manumission, although they are not incidental in other matters, such as testimony, inheritance, and others.
And his saying, peace be upon him: "No judge should judge between two while he is angry," there is no doubt that it indicates the prohibition of a judge judging in every state by which confusion arises that prevents full consideration, such as excessive hunger and thirst, excessive joy and sorrow, and needing to urinate or defecate excessively.
And his prohibition, peace be upon him, of urinating in stagnant water: there is no doubt that it indicates the prohibition of urinating into a bottle, for example, and pouring urine from the bottle into stagnant water; for there is no difference that affects the ruling between urinating into it directly and pouring it into it from a bottle or the like. Examples of this are very numerous, and none can oppose them except the obstinate. And there is no doubt that all of that is reasoning from what is stated to what is silent about. Likewise, the type of ijtihad known in the terminology of the jurists of usul as "tahqiq al-manat" (verifying the cause) cannot be denied except by the obstinate, and its issues on which disagreement is impossible for anyone other than the obstinate are not confined by enumeration; and we will mention examples of them. Among that is His saying: ﴿Judged by it are two just men among you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]; so the fact that the killed game is matched by a specific kind of livestock is ijtihad in verifying the cause (manat) of this ruling, which Allah the Exalted stated in His firm Book, and it is conclusive evidence against the claim of whoever makes ijtihad in the Sharia impossible from its root. And maintenance of wives is obligatory, and determining the required amount necessarily involves a kind of ijtihad in verifying the cause of that ruling. The values of destroyed property are obligatory upon the one who destroyed it, and determining the required amount necessarily involves ijtihad. Zakat is not spent except on its recipients, such as the poor, and their poverty is not known except through presumptive indicators, which are sought through circumstantial evidence; because the reality of the inner state is known only to Allah, and one is not judged except by the word of a just person, and his justice is known only through presumptive indicators sought through circumstantial evidence of dealings, giving and taking, and long association. Likewise, the ijtihad of travelers regarding the direction of the qiblah by signs, and so on with what cannot be counted.
Among the texts indicating the legitimacy of ijtihad in matters of the Sharia is what is established in the Sahih from the Prophet ﷺ regarding that. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: Yahya ibn Yahya al-Tamimi narrated to us, Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad informed us, from Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Usamah ibn al-Had, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, from Busr ibn Sa'id, from Abu Qays, client of Amr ibn al-As, from Amr ibn al-As, that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "When a judge judges and strives (ijtahada), then is correct, he has two rewards; and when he judges and strives, then errs, he has one reward."

And Ishaq ibn Ibrahim and Muhammad ibn Abi Umar both narrated to me from Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad with this chain the like of it, and added at the end of the hadith: Yazid said: I narrated this hadith to Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Hazm, and he said: "Thus Abu Salamah narrated to me, from Abu Hurayrah." And Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Darimi narrated to me: Marwan – meaning Ibn Muhammad al-Dimashqi – informed us, al-Layth ibn Sa'd narrated to us, Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Usamah ibn al-Had al-Laythi narrated to me this hadith, like the narration of Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad with both chains together. End of quote.

This is an authentic text from the Prophet ﷺ, explicit in permitting ijtihad in the legal rulings, and in obtaining reward for it even if the one who strives is mistaken in his ijtihad, and this decisively cuts off the claim of the Zahiriyyah that ijtihad is prohibited from its root, and declaring its doer and the one who holds it misguided, conclusively, as you see.

And al-Nawawi said in explaining this hadith: The scholars said: The Muslims agreed that this hadith concerns a judge who is a scholar and qualified to judge; if he is correct, he has two rewards: a reward for his ijtihad, and a reward for his correctness; and if he errs, he has a reward for his ijtihad. In the hadith there is an omitted element, its implied meaning being: when the judge intends to judge and strives. They said: As for one who is not qualified to judge, it is not lawful for him to judge; if he judges, he has no reward, rather he is sinful, and his judgment is not valid whether it agrees with the truth or not; because his correctness is coincidental, not issuing from a legal basis, so he is disobedient in all his rulings whether they agree with the right or not, and they are all rejected, and he is not excused in any of that. And there has come in a hadith in the Sunan: "Judges are three: a judge in Paradise, and two in the Fire. A judge who knew the truth and judged by it is in Paradise; a judge who knew the truth and judged contrary to it is in the Fire; and a judge who judged in ignorance is in the Fire." End of the purpose of al-Nawawi's words.

If it is said: The ijtihad mentioned in the hadith is ijtihad in verifying the cause (tahqiq al-manat) only, to the exclusion of other types of ijtihad.

The answer: This is diverting his words, peace be upon him, from their apparent meaning without evidence that requires recourse to it, and that is impermissible.

(p-150) Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Chapter: The reward of a judge who exercises ijtihad (independent reasoning) and is correct or mistaken." 'Abdullah ibn Yazid narrated to us: Haywah narrated to us: Yazid ibn 'Abdullah ibn al-Had told me, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith, from Busr ibn Sa'id, from Abu Qays, the client (mawla) of 'Amr ibn al-'As, from 'Amr ibn al-'As, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When a judge judges, exercises ijtihad, and is correct, he has two rewards; and when he judges, exercises ijtihad, and is mistaken, he has one reward." He (Abu Qays) said: "I narrated this hadith to Abu Bakr ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, and he said: 'Thus Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to me, from Abu Hurayrah.'" 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn al-Muttalib said, from 'Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr, from Abu Salamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it. End of quotation.

This hadith, agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh), proves the invalidity of the view of those who deny ijtihad altogether in the legal rulings of the Shari'ah. As for Ibn Hazm's attempt to weaken this agreed-upon hadith, which you have seen is in the highest rank of sahih because both Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) agreed upon it, there is no need to refute it, since its failure is evident as you see; for it is an agreed-upon hadith, narrated through sound chains from two eminent Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Among the proofs for this is what is related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him): "When the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen, he said to him: 'By what will you judge?' He said: 'By the Book of Allah.' He said: 'And if you do not find it?' He said: 'By the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' He said: 'And if you do not find it?' He said: 'I will exercise my own opinion (ajtahidu ra'yi).' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck his chest and said: 'Praise be to Allah who has granted success to the messenger of the Messenger of Allah with what pleases the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'"

Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) said in the introduction to his Tafsir, after mentioning this hadith, the following: "This hadith is in the Musnad and the Sunan with a good (jayyid) chain, as is established in its proper place."

Ibn Qudamah said (in Rawdat al-Nazir), after citing this hadith: "They (the critics) said: 'This hadith is narrated by al-Harith ibn 'Amr from men of Homs, and al-Harith and the men are unknown (majhul); so said al-Tirmidhi.' We say: It has been narrated by 'Ubadah ibn Nusayy, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, from Mu'adh (may Allah be pleased with him)." End of quotation.

The meaning of Ibn Qudamah is clear, because the Zahiriyyah's rejection of this hadith on the basis of the unknown status of its narrator from Mu'adh is refuted by the fact that 'Ubadah ibn Nusayy narrated it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm from him (Mu'adh). This narration is not what Ibn Kathir meant by his saying "this hadith is in the Musnad and the Sunan with a good chain," because it is not in the Musnad nor in the (p-151) Sunan. Perhaps his intended meaning by the goodness of this chain is that al-Harith, the nephew of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, was deemed reliable (thiqah) by Ibn Hibban, and that the companions of Mu'adh are regarded by him as upright (udul), none of them being impugned or accused. The thorough investigation of the routes of this hadith will come in Surat al-Anbiya'. It is known that 'Ubadah ibn Nusayy is a reliable and virtuous narrator, as we previously mentioned. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm is said to be a Companion; al-Ijli mentioned him among the senior reliable Successors (kibar thiqat al-tabi'in), as stated in al-Taqrib. The hadith of Mu'adh has been received with acceptance by the Community (ummah), in past and present times. What the people of knowledge have used as evidence for this from the verses of the Great Qur'an will come, Allah willing, in "Surat al-Anbiya'" and "Surat al-Hashr."

Among the proofs that attaching a like case to its like in the Shari'ah is permissible (ilhaq al-nazir bi-nazirihi, i.e., analogical reasoning, qiyas) is what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their two Sahihs from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "A woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my mother has died and she owed a vow of fasting; shall I fast on her behalf?' He said: 'What do you think, if your mother had a debt and you paid it, would that have discharged it for her?' She said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then fast on behalf of your mother.'" In another narration from them both, from him, he said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my mother has died and she owed a month of fasting; shall I make it up on her behalf?' He said: 'If your mother had a debt, would you have paid it on her behalf?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'The debt of Allah is more deserving of being paid.'" End of quotation.

The variation in the narration of this hadith does not count as idtirab (confusion in transmission), because these are multiple incidents: a woman asked him and he gave her a ruling, and a man asked him and he gave him a ruling like the one he gave the woman, as several scholars have pointed out.

This is an authentic explicit text from the Prophet (ﷺ), clear in establishing the legitimacy of attaching a like case to its like that shares the same effective cause ('illah) of the ruling; for he (ﷺ) made explicit the attachment of the debt of Allah the Exalted to the debt owed to a human being, on the common ground that both are a right that may be demanded, and the demand is discharged by paying it to its rightful recipient. This is clearly evident as a proof for analogy (qiyas), as you see.

Among the proofs for this also is what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) also recorded in their two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "A man from the Banu Fazarah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'My wife has given birth to a black boy!' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do you have camels?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What are their colors?' He said: 'Red.' He said: 'Are there any grey (awraq) among them?' He said: 'Indeed, there are some grey among them.' He said: 'Then how did that come about?' He said: 'Perhaps a vein (irq) drew it out.' He said: 'And this (child) perhaps has a vein that drew it out.'" End of quotation.

This is an authentic explicit text from the Prophet (ﷺ), clear in the analogy of a like case to its like. A legal ruling has resulted from this analogy: that a child's blackness, alongside the whiteness of his father and mother, does not necessitate li'an (mutual oath of condemnation); (p-152) he (ﷺ) did not make his blackness an indication that she had committed adultery with a black man, since it is possible that among his ancestors there was someone black, and the blackness of that grandfather was drawn out in him. Likewise, those red camels contain grey camels, and it is possible that they have grey ancestors whose colors drew them toward greyness. With this the questioner was convinced.

Among the proofs for attaching a like case to its like is what Abu Dawud, the Imam Ahmad, and al-Nasa'i recorded from 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I was aroused one day and kissed (my wife) while I was fasting. I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Today I have done a great thing! I kissed while I was fasting!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What do you think, if you rinsed your mouth with water while you were fasting?' I said: 'There is no harm in that.' He (ﷺ) said: 'Then what (is the difference)?'" End of quotation.

It may be objected: al-Nasa'i said about this hadith: "munkar" (rejected).

We reply: Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim authenticated it. So said al-Shawkani in Nayl al-Awtar.

The author of this (commentary), may Allah pardon him, says: This hadith is established and its chain is sound. Abu Dawud said in his Sunan: "Ahmad ibn Yunus narrated to us, al-Layth narrated to us (ḥ), and 'Isa ibn Hammad narrated to us, al-Layth ibn Sa'd informed us, from Bukayr ibn 'Abdullah, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id, from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: I was aroused and kissed..." up to the end of the hadith with its wording mentioned above. It is not hidden that this chain is sound, for its first tier is Ahmad ibn Yunus and 'Isa ibn Hammad. As for Ahmad, he is Ibn 'Abdullah ibn Yunus al-Kufi al-Tamimi al-Yarbu'i, reliable and a memorizer (thiqah hafiz). 'Isa ibn Hammad al-Tujibi, Abu Musa al-Ansari, known by the epithet Zughbah, is reliable. Its second tier is al-Layth ibn Sa'd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Fahmi, Abu al-Harith al-Misri, reliable and firm, a jurist and renowned imam. Its third tier is Bukayr ibn 'Abdullah ibn al-Ashajj, client of the Banu Makhzum, Abu 'Abdullah or Abu Yusuf al-Madani, resident of Egypt; reliable. Its fourth tier is 'Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id ibn Suwayd al-Ansari al-Madani, reliable. Its fifth tier is Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, from the Prophet (ﷺ). So this is a sound chain whose narrators are reliable, as you see. It is an authentic and explicit text that he (ﷺ) analogized kissing to rinsing the mouth, for rinsing the mouth is a preliminary to drinking, and kissing is a preliminary to intercourse; the common factor between them is that each is a preliminary to breaking the fast, and in itself neither breaks the fast.

These proofs that we have mentioned contain clear evidence that attaching a like case to its like in the Shari'ah has no opponent, because he (ﷺ) did it; and Allah says: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21]; and he (ﷺ) did not do it except to alert the people to it.

(p-153) If it is objected: "He (ﷺ) did that only because Allah revealed that to him."

We reply: His action is a proof for doing the like of what he did. Even if he did it by revelation, like all his other sayings, actions, and tacit approvals, all of these establish proof, even if he (ﷺ) did what he did of that by revelation from Allah the Exalted.

* *

Issue (masalah)

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad, one of the scholars of the Malikis, said: "This verse includes a ruling on judgment by qafah (physiognomic tracking/ascertaining lineage by resemblance). For when He said: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra': 36], it indicates the permissibility of what we have knowledge of; so whatever a person knows or whose probability (zann) predominates for him, it is permissible for him to judge by it. By this we have argued for establishing the lot (qur'ah) and estimation (kharṣ), for it is a kind of predominance of probability, and it is sometimes called knowledge by extension. The qa'if (tracker) attributes the child to his father through the resemblance between them, just as the jurist attaches the derivative branch to its root through resemblance." In the Sahih, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her): "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon me joyful, his face's creases shining, and said: 'Did you not see that Mujazziz al-Mudlaji just now looked at Zayd ibn Harithah and Usamah ibn Zayd, and they were covered with a cloak, their heads covered and their feet exposed, and he said: Indeed some of these feet are from others.'" And in the hadith of Yunus ibn Yazid: "Mujazziz was a qa'if." End of quotation, through al-Qurtubi's transmission in his Tafsir.

The author of this (commentary), may Allah pardon him, says: It is well known that the scholars differed regarding the consideration of the statements of the qafah. Some held that they are not considered, and those who argued for non-consideration cited the story of the Ansari woman who performed li'an against her husband and bore a child very similar to the man she was accused of with, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not consider this resemblance; so he did not rule that the child was from fornication, nor did he flog the woman.

They said: If resemblance established lineage, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have established by it that that child was from that man she was accused of, and it would necessarily follow that the hadd punishment be enforced on her and that the child be judged the son of fornication; but the Prophet (ﷺ) did none of that, as will be made clear (in Surat al-Nur), Allah willing.

This view of not considering the statements of the qafah is reported from Abu Hanifah, Ishaq, al-Thawri, and their companions.

The majority of the people of knowledge held that the statements of the qafah are considered when disputes arise concerning a child, citing what is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of 'A'ishah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was pleased with the statement of Mujazziz ibn al-A'war al-Mudlaji: 'Indeed some of these feet are from others,' until the creases of his face shone with joy."

They said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would not have been pleased with falsehood nor would he have approved of it; rather, his pleasure at the statement of the qafah is evidence that it is from the truth and not from falsehood. For his tacit approval alone suffices for the legitimacy of what he approved; and more so if his pleasure in the matter exceeded mere approval, which is clear as you see.

Know that those who said the statements of the qafah are considered differed: Some said that this is accepted only for the children of slave women, not for the children of free women. Others said that it is accepted for all.

The author of this (commentary), may Allah pardon him, says: The verified view is to consider it for the children of both free women and slave women; for the Prophet's (ﷺ) pleasure occurred regarding the child of a free woman, and the case of the cause of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is definitive in its inclusion, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence. This is the view of the majority and it is the truth, in contrast to Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him), who said that the case of the cause is speculative in its inclusion. The author of Maraqi al-Su'ud summarized this in his verse:

"Affirm definitively the inclusion of the entities of the cause, and narrate from the Imam the speculative (view), and you will be correct."

* *

Two remarks (tanbihan)

The First: Statements of the qā'if (the physiognomists who read lineage from resemblance) are not taken into account regarding a child's resemblance to a man if the child's mother is a bed (firāsh) for another man. This is because the Prophet ﷺ saw the strong resemblance of the child over which Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abd ibn Zam'ah disputed, to 'Utbah ibn Abi Waqqas, yet this resemblance had no effect on his lineage, since the mother of the child was a bed for Zam'ah. So he ﷺ said: "The child belongs to the bed, and for the fornicator is the stone." However, he ﷺ took this resemblance into account in another respect other than lineage, for he said to Sawdah bint Zam'ah, may Allah be pleased with her: "Veil yourself from him," even though he had attributed the child to her father, so he never saw Sawdah at all. This matter is a principle among the Malikis in the consideration of disagreement (murā'āt al-khilāf), as is well known among them.

* *

The Second Admonition

Some of the scholars of Arabic said: The original meaning of qafw is slander (buht) and false accusation (qadhf) with what is untrue, and from it is the hadith narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "We are the sons of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah; we do not accuse our mother (of adultery) and we do not deny our father." It was recorded by Imam Ahmad, Ibn Majah and others from the hadith of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays, and Ibn Kathir in his History collected the chains of this hadith. His saying "we do not qafw our mother" means we do not slander our mother and revile her. From it is the saying of al-Kumayt:

"So I do not shoot the innocent without fault, nor do I qafw the chaste women if we are qafw-ed."

And the saying of al-Nabighah al-Ja'di: (p-155)

"And like the dolls are the proud-nosed ones, with modesty dwelling in them, they do not spread the qafāfī (slanders)."

What appears to us is that the original meaning of qafw in the language of the Arabs is following (ittibā'), as is known from the lexicon, and it includes following of evils, as mentioned by the one who said its origin is slander and buhtān.

* *

As for His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned about﴾ [al-Isra' 36], there are two interpretations:

The first: The meaning of the verse is that a person will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about the deeds of his limbs, and it will be said to him: Why did you listen to what it was not permissible for you to listen to? Why did you look at what it was not permissible for you to look at? Why did you resolve upon what it was not permissible for you to resolve upon?

Verses of Allah's Book indicate this meaning, such as His saying: ﴿And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 93], and His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all, about what they used to do﴾ [al-Hijr 92-93], and similar verses.

The second interpretation: The limbs are those that will be questioned about the deeds of their owner, so his limbs will bear witness against him to what he did.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: This meaning is more eloquent in argument, for his denial comes from his own limbs, and that is the utmost disgrace, as He said: ﴿Today We seal over their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn﴾ [Ya-Sin 65], and His saying: ﴿Their hearing, their sight, and their skins will bear witness against them to what they used to do﴾ [Fussilat 20].

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: The first view appears more correct to me, and it is the view of the majority.

In this noble verse there is a subtle point that he indicated in other places: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned about﴾ [al-Isra' 36] indicates the reason for the prohibition in His saying: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra' 36], by being questioned about the aforementioned limbs, based on what is established in the principles of jurisprudence regarding the method of indication and alerting (al-īmā' wal-tanbīh): that the particle "inna" with a kasra is one of the particles of causation (ta'līl). Its clarification: the meaning is: desist from what is not permissible for you, because Allah has blessed you with hearing, sight, and intellect so that you may be thankful to Him, and He tests you with them and will question you about them, so do not use His blessings in disobedience.

This meaning is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the bellies of your mothers, knowing nothing, and made for you hearing and sight and hearts, that you may be grateful﴾ [al-Nahl 78], and similar verses. (p-156)

The reference in His saying in this noble verse, "ulā'ika" (those), returns to ﴿the hearing, the sight, and the heart﴾, and this is evidence that "ulā'ika" is used as a demonstrative for non-rational beings, which is the correct view. Among its evidences in Arabic is the saying of the poet al-Arji:

"Oh, how lovely are the gazelles that grazed for us among those acacias and mimosas of yours!"

And the saying of Jarir:

"He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and the life after those days."

This is in contrast to one who claimed that Jarir's verse has no evidence in it, and that the reading in it is "after those peoples." And Allah knows best.

His Exalted Majesty forbids people in this noble verse from arrogance and strutting in their gait. His words "مَرَحًا" (*marahan*, "exultantly") [al-Isra: 37] are an indefinite verbal noun (masdar munakkar) functioning as a circumstantial accusative (hal), following the rule of Ibn Malik in the *Khulasah* (al-Alfiyya):

*"An indefinite verbal noun may come as a circumstantial, frequently, like 'baghtatan' (suddenly) in 'Zayd came out suddenly.'"*

It has also been read as "مَرِحًا" (*marihan*) with a kasra on the ra', as an adjective from *marih* (yamrah, with a fatha), meaning: do not walk on the earth while you are swaggering, strutting like the tyrants.

His Exalted Majesty has clarified this meaning in other places, such as His words, addressing Luqman as an instruction to him: ﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people, and do not walk on the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like every arrogant boaster.﴾ ﴿And be moderate in your walking﴾ [Luqman: 18-19], and His words: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], among other verses.

The root meaning of *marah* in the language is intense joy and vigor. Applying it to a person's walk in a swaggering manner like the arrogant is because that is usually among the consequences of intense joy and vigor.

In my view, the more correct of the two opinions regarding His words ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 37] is that its meaning is: you will never make a rift in it by your treading upon it and the force of your stamping on it. This meaning is supported by His following words: ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾ [al-Isra: 37], meaning: you, O arrogant haughty one, are weak, insignificant, powerless, confined between two inanimate things. You are unable to affect them. The earth beneath you cannot be affected so as to be torn by the force of your stamping on it, and the lofty mountains above you, your height cannot reach their height. So know your worth, do not be arrogant, and do not walk on the earth exultantly. (p-157) 

The second opinion is that the meaning of ﴿you will never tear through the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 37] is: you will never cross it by your walking. This was said by Ibn Jarir, who cited as evidence the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

*"And a dark, deep, empty desert crossed (al-mukhtaraq), its landmarks confused, its mirages flashing."*

This is because his intended meaning by *al-mukhtaraq* is the place of crossing, i.e., the walking and passing through it.

The best grammatical parsing (i'rab) of His words "طُولًا" (*tulan*, "in height") is that it is a tamyiz muhawwal (a transferred specification accusative) from the subject, meaning: your height will never reach the mountains. This differs from those who parse it as a circumstantial accusative (hal), and from those who parse it as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Someone has excellently said:

*"Do not walk above the earth except in humility, for beneath it are many people who are higher than you. And even if you are in might, protection and strength, many people have died who were more mighty than you."*

Some scholars have used His words ﴿And do not walk on the earth exultantly﴾ [al-Isra: 37] as evidence for prohibiting dancing and engaging in it, because the one who dances is among those who walk exultantly.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 40:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons and taken for Himself daughters from the angels? Indeed, you utter a monstrous saying.﴾

The hamzah (the interrogative particle) in His saying ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons﴾ [al-Isra': 40] is for rebuke (*inkar*). The meaning of the verse is: Has your Lord singled you out, with special favour and preference, with the best of offspring, who are the sons, leaving no share of them for Himself, while taking for Himself the lesser of them, which are the daughters? This is contrary to reason and custom, for masters do not give their slaves the finest and purest of things and take for themselves the worst and lowest. So if the Majestic and Exalted were to take a son, exalted is He far above that, to a great height, then He would have taken the better of the two shares and not the worse, and He would not have chosen you over Himself with the better of the two.

This rebuke is directed at the disbelievers in their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, exalted is He far above what they say, to a great height. They have attributed offspring to Him, and yet they have attributed to Him the weakest and worst of them, which is females, while they themselves do not accept them for themselves.

Allah the Exalted has clarified this meaning in many verses, such as:

• His saying: ﴿For you is the male and for Him the female? That, then, is an unjust division.﴾ [al-Najm: 21–22]

• His saying: ﴿Or has He taken daughters over sons?﴾

• His saying: ﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen whatever He willed from what He creates.﴾ [al-Zumar: 4]. The verses of this kind are very numerous, and we have explained this clearly in the commentary on "Surat al-Nahl." His saying in this noble verse, ﴿Indeed, you utter a monstrous saying﴾ [al-Isra': 40] (p-158), indicates that attributing offspring to Allah, exalted is He far above that, to a great height, is an exceedingly grave matter. He has shown how great its gravity is

• by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Certainly you have produced a thing terrible. The heavens are nearly rent therefrom, the earth splits open, and the mountains fall in ruin, that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son. And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son. There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a slave. He has enumerated them and counted them precisely. And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.﴾ [Maryam: 88–95]. The polytheists, may Allah disfigure them, made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, into females, then claimed that they are the daughters of Allah, then worshipped them. Thus they committed the greatest crime in three stages.

As for the hamzah and the fa' (conjunction) in phrases such as His saying ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you﴾ [al-Isra': 40], we have also explained their ruling clearly in "Surat al-Nahl."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Had there been with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.﴾

The majority of reciters read "كَما تَقُولُونَ" (kamā taqūlūna, "as you say") with the second-person address (tā' al-khiṭāb). Ibn Kathir and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read ﴿كَما يَقُولُونَ﴾ [al-Isra': 42] (kamā yaqūlūna, "as they say") with the third-person (yā' al-ghaybah). There are two interpretations of the meaning of this noble verse, both of which are true and both of which are supported by the Qur'an. We have already mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that a verse may have two interpretations, both true and both supported by the Qur'an, so we mention all of them, since all of it is true.

The first of the two mentioned interpretations: the meaning of the noble verse is: Had there been with Allah other gods, as the disbelievers claim, they (i.e., the supposed gods) would have sought (i.e., would have sought) to the Lord of the Throne (i.e., to Allah) a way; that is, a way to overpower Him and remove His dominion, because they would then be His partners, just as kings act with one another. Glory be to Allah, exalted far above that!

This explanation of the verse is the apparent one in my view, and it is what comes first to mind from the meaning of the noble verse. Among the verses that bear witness to this meaning is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there is not with Him any god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others. Glory be to Allah above what they describe.﴾ ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; so exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91-92], and His saying: ﴿Had there been in them (the heavens and the earth) gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined. So exalted is Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. This meaning of the verse is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, al-Naqqash, Abu Mansur, and others among the theologians.

The second interpretation of the noble verse: the meaning is ﴿they would have sought to the Lord of the Throne a way﴾ (p-159), that is, a path and a means that brings them close to Him, in acknowledgment of His grace. This meaning is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek means of access to their Lord, [striving to be] nearest, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾ [al-Isra': 57], and the verse continues. This view is narrated from Qatadah, and Ibn Kathir confined himself to it in his tafsir.

There is no doubt that the apparent meaning that comes first to mind from the verse according to the Arabic language is the first view, because the verse posits a hypothetical impossibility, and the supposed impossibility, namely the existence of gods sharing with Allah, does not appear with it to be seeking nearness to Him; rather, if they existed they would contend with Him. But they are non-existent and impossible to exist, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 45:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾

In this noble verse there are two interpretations (wajhan min al-tafsir):

The first: the meaning is ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a barrier﴾; that is, a obstruction (ha'il) and a veil (satir) that prevents them from understanding the Qur'an and comprehending it, lest they grasp it and benefit from it. According to this view, the "hidden barrier" (hijab mastur) is that with which Allah has veiled their hearts from benefiting from His Book. The verses that bear witness to this meaning are many:

• such as His saying: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings from what you invite us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier, so work, indeed we are working"﴾ [Fussilat: 5],

• and His saying: ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], to the end of the verse,

• and His saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it﴾ [al-Kahf: 57], to the end of the verse,

in addition to other verses. Among those who held this view regarding the meaning of the verse are Qatadah, al-Zajjaj, and others.

The second interpretation of the verse: the intended meaning of the "hidden barrier" is that Allah conceals it from the eyes of the disbelievers, so they do not see it. The author of al-Durr al-Manthur, in discussing this verse, said: Abu Ya'la and Ibn Abi Hatim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi together in al-Dala'il, related from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that she said: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad: 1], Umm Jamil al-'Awra' came, wailing, with a stone in her hand, saying:

We have disobeyed the one reviled (mudhammaman), we have rejected him, and we have disobeyed his command.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting, and Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was beside him. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "This woman has come, and I fear she will see you." He said: "She will not see me." He recited a Qur'an with which he sought protection, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾ (p-160) [al-Isra': 45]. She came until she stood over Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), but she did not see the Prophet (ﷺ). She said: "O Abu Bakr, I have been told that your companion has satirized me." Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirized you." She departed, saying: "Quraysh already knows that I am the daughter of its chief," in addition to other narrations with this meaning.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse, after citing some narrations similar to what we have mentioned in this last interpretation, the following text: "There happened to me in our land, al-Andalus, in the fortress of Manthur in the districts of Cordoba, something similar to this. I fled from the enemy and withdrew to a side away from it. Before long, two horsemen came out in pursuit of me, while I was sitting in an open area of the earth with nothing shielding me from them, reciting the beginning of Surah Ya-Sin and other parts of the Qur'an. They passed by me, then returned from whence they had come, and one of them said to the other: 'This is a dibla' (meaning a devil), and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, blinded their sight so they did not see me." End of quotation. Al-Qurtubi said: this interpretation of the verse is the most apparent.

And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿hidden barrier (hijaban mastura)﴾, some scholars said: it is from the use of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul) in the sense of the active participle (ism al-fa'il); that is, a concealing barrier (hijaban satiran). The reverse may also occur, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from a gushing water (min ma'in daafiq)﴾ [al-Tariq: 6], meaning gushing (madfuq); ﴿a pleasing life (ishatin radiyatin)﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21], meaning pleasing (mardiyyah). The use of each of the active and passive participle in the sense of the other is one of the methods of the Arabic language, and the rhetoricians (al-bayaniyyun) call such usage "rational metaphor" (majaz 'aqli). Among examples of using the passive participle to mean the active is what is said in the verse: "maymun" and "mash'um," meaning blessed (yamin) and ill-omened (sha'im). Some scholars said: His saying ﴿mastura﴾ is according to its apparent meaning as a passive participle, because that barrier is hidden from people's eyes so they do not see it, or the reciter is hidden by it so no one other than him sees him. Abu Hayyan adopted this in al-Bahr, and knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 46:

Allah's saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, makes clear that He placed over the hearts of the disbelievers coverings (plural of kinan), which is that which conceals a thing, shields it and wraps it up, so that they do not understand the Qur'an, or out of aversion to their understanding it, because those coverings stand between their hearts and the understanding of the Qur'an, that is, comprehending its meanings in a way that benefits its possessor. And He placed in their ears deafness (waqr), that is, dullness and heaviness, so that they do not hear it with the hearing of acceptance and benefit.

In other places He has made clear the cause of the barrier between the hearts and benefiting from it, and that it is their disbelief. (p-161) So Allah requited them for their disbelief with the obliteration of insight, the turning away of hearts, sealing, the stamping (ṭab') and the seals and coverings that prevent good from reaching them, such as:

• His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff: 5],

• and His saying: ﴿Nay, Allah has sealed it upon them because of their disbelief﴾ [An-Nisa: 155],

• and His saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [Al-An'am: 110],

• and His saying: ﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah increased them in disease﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 10],

• and His saying: ﴿And as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to them filth upon their filth, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [At-Tawbah: 125],

and other verses.

Reminder

In this noble verse there is a clear refutation of the Qadariyyah in their saying that evil does not occur by the will of Allah, but by the will of the servant. Glory be to Allah, and exalted is He far above that anything should occur in His dominion without His will. ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have associated﴾ [Al-An'am: 107], ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [As-Sajdah: 13], ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [Al-An'am: 35], and other verses.

* *

Allah's saying: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn away on their backs in aversion.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, makes clear that when His Prophet ﷺ mentions his Lord alone in the Qur'an, by saying: "There is no deity but Allah," the disbelievers turn away on their backs in aversion, out of hatred for the word of tawhid and love for associating others with Him, Mighty and Majestic.

He clarified this meaning in other places, making clear that their aversion from the mention of Him alone, Mighty and Majestic, is the cause of their abiding in the Fire:

• Such as His saying: ﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink, but when those besides Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice﴾ [Az-Zumar: 45],

• and His saying: ﴿That is because when Allah was invoked alone, you disbelieved, but when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Most Great﴾ [Ghafir: 12],

• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, they, when it was said to them, "There is no deity but Allah," were arrogant﴾ ﴿and said, "Shall we leave our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ [As-Saffat: 35, 36],

• and His saying: ﴿Grievous to the polytheists is that to which you invite them﴾ [Ash-Shura: 13],

• and His saying: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear evidence, you recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial; they nearly attack those who recite to them Our verses﴾ [Al-Hajj: 72],

• and His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and speak over it, that you may overcome"﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

His saying in this verse: nufūran [Al-Isra: 46] is the plural of nāfir; it is then a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). That is: they turned away on their backs while being averse to the mention of Allah alone without associating anything with Him. The active participle (fā'il) is pluralized as fu'ūl, like sājid and sujūd, and rāki' and rukū'.

Some scholars said: "nufūran" is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and accordingly it takes the place of the absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) of His saying "they turned away," because turning away from the mention of Him alone means aversion from it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides Him; they do not possess the removal of harm from you, nor its transfer.﴾ ﴿Those whom they call upon seek their way to their Lord, (as to) which of them is nearer, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared.﴾

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, makes clear that the objects of worship besides Allah, whom the disbelievers claimed would bring them near to Allah in closeness and intercede for them with Him, do not possess the removal of harm from their worshippers, that is, the removal of what is disliked from them, nor "transfer" (taḥwīlan), that is, transferring it from one person to another, or transferring illness to health, poverty to wealth, drought to fertility, and the like. Then He makes clear in it also that the objects of worship whom the disbelievers worshipped besides Allah are themselves seeking nearness to Allah through obedience to Him, and seeking the means (al-wasīlah) to Him, that is, the path to His pleasure and the attainment of what is with Him of reward through obedience to Him. So it was obligatory upon you that you should be like them.

Ibn Mas'ud said: this verse was revealed concerning a group of Arabs from Khuza'ah, or others, who used to worship men of the jinn. Then the jinn became Muslim, and the disbelievers remained worshipping them, so Allah revealed: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek their way to their Lord﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Isra: 57]. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse was revealed concerning those who used to worship 'Uzayr, al-Masih and his mother. And it is also related from him, and from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Zayd, and al-Hasan, that it was revealed concerning the worshippers of the angels. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning the worshippers of the sun, the moon, the stars, 'Uzayr, al-Masih and his mother.

This meaning which He, majestic and exalted, has made clear in this noble verse, namely that every object of worship besides Allah does not benefit its worshipper, and that every object of worship besides Him is in need of Him and dependent upon Him, majestic and exalted, He has also made clear in other places, such as His saying in Saba': ﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides Allah; they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have any share in them, nor is there for Him any helper among them.﴾ ﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba': 22-23], and His saying in az-Zumar: ﴿Have you considered what you call upon besides Allah? If Allah should intend me with harm, could they remove His harm? Or if He should intend me with mercy, could they withhold His mercy? Say: Sufficient for me is Allah; upon Him rely the reliant.﴾ [az-Zumar: 38], and other verses besides these.

We have previously mentioned in the surah of al-Ma'idah that what is meant by "al-wasilah" in this noble verse, and in the verse of al-Ma'idah, is drawing near to Allah through righteous deeds. From it is the saying of Labid:

Do I see people not knowing the worth of their affair? Yes, every person of intellect is one who seeks means to Allah.

We have also previously mentioned in al-Ma'idah that the verified view is that the saying of 'Antarah:

Indeed, men have a means (wasilah) to you; if they take you, then adorn yourself with kohl and dye.

is from this meaning, as we previously mentioned that its plural is wasa'il, as in his saying:

When the slanderers are heedless, we return to our union, and the closeness between us and the means (al-wasa'il) returns.

The most correct grammatical analysis of His saying: ﴿(as to) which of them is nearer﴾ [al-Isra: 57], is that it is a substitute (badal) for the waw of the subject in His saying "yabtaghun" (they seek). We have clarified this in the surah of al-Ma'idah in a manner that suffices from repeating it here. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is no town but We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection, or punish it with a severe punishment. That is written in the Book as a decree.﴾

Some of the people of knowledge (ahl al-'ilm) said: In this noble verse there is an omission of a qualifier (ṣifah), i.e., "And there is no unjust town but We will destroy it." This omitted qualifier is indicated by verses of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, such as:

• His saying: ﴿We never destroyed the towns except when their people were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Qasas: 59],

• and His saying: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are unaware﴾ [al-An'am: 131], meaning: rather, the messengers must warn them, so they disbelieve in them and in their Lord,

• and His saying: ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hud: 117],

• and His saying: ﴿And how many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We called it to a severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment. So it tasted the consequence of its affair, and the outcome of its affair was loss﴾ [al-Talaq: 8, 9],

and other verses besides these.

The most that can be said for this view is that a qualifier is omitted while there are proofs indicating it. Its parallel in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿And behind them was a king who seized every boat by force﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning every sound boat. The evidence for this is that the hole made in the boat by al-Khidr, in which he and Musa had embarked, was intended to preserve it from the king's seizure, because he would not seize a defective boat containing a hole, but only a sound one. Among omissions of a qualifier is His saying: ﴿They said, "Now you have brought the truth"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71], meaning: the clear truth with no ambiguity regarding the required attributes of the cow. A parallel from the speech of the Arabs is the verse of the poet, who is al-Muraqqish al-Akbar:

"And many a soft-cheeked maiden, a virgin, slender, who has a dark tress and a long neck"

meaning: a dark (fāḥim) tress and a long neck.

And the saying of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

"Whoever's word is a word, and whoever's deed is a deed, and whoever's gift is a gift"

meaning: his word is a decisive word, his deed is a beautiful deed, and his gift is a generous gift. To this the author of the Khulasah alluded in his saying:

"The qualifier may be omitted from the qualified when understood, and omitting the qualifier is rare"

Some of the people of knowledge said: The verse is general. So the righteous town's destruction is by death, and the wicked town's destruction is by punishment. There is no doubt that every soul shall taste death. By "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and "masṭūr" means "written." From this is the saying of Jarir:

"Whoever wishes, I will sell him my wealth and my ... such that the Taym in its register cannot complete a line"
